moments.title: Newton's annus mirabilis
moments.body:
Cambridge closes due to the plague. Newton, age 22, returns home to Lincolnshire. Over 18 months he develops his theory of colours, the binomial theorem, the calculus, and the inverse-square law of gravitation.

He does not publish. The famous apple story (told decades later) places the gravity insight in his mother's garden at Woolsthorpe. He compares the falling apple to the falling Moon and asks whether the same force acts on both.

quote.text: I began to think of gravity extending to the orb of the Moon... All this was in the two plague years of 1665 and 1666, for in those days I was in the prime of my age for invention.

moments.takeaway: The most productive period in the history of physics — and Newton publishes none of it for two decades.

moments.title: Halley's visit to Cambridge
moments.body:
Halley, Wren and Hooke have been arguing about whether elliptical planetary orbits could be derived from an inverse-square force law. None of them can do the maths. Halley visits Newton and asks the question.

Newton replies that he had worked it out years ago but mislaid the proof. Halley persuades him to redo and publish the work. Three years later the Principia Mathematica appears, with Halley funding the publication out of his own pocket.
moments.takeaway: Without Halley's persistence, the Principia might never have been written.

moments.title: The Principia
moments.body:
Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica is published in Latin. It contains the three laws of motion, the universal law of gravitation (F = G m1 m2 over r squared), and demonstrations that Kepler's laws follow from those.

Newton's mathematics is geometric (Euclidean), not the modern calculus notation. Subsequent generations recast his arguments in differential equations.

quote.text: Hypotheses non fingo.
quote.attrib: Newton — 'I frame no hypotheses' — on refusing to speculate about the underlying cause of gravity

moments.takeaway: Mechanics becomes a quantitative, predictive science. Physics has its founding text.

moments.title: Einstein's general relativity
moments.body:
Newton's gravity is a force at a distance, instantaneous and inexplicable. Einstein recasts gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass-energy. Massless light is bent by gravity. Mercury's perihelion precession (43 arcseconds per century unexplained by Newton) is predicted exactly.

The theory is published in the depths of WWI. Confirmation comes in 1919 when Eddington measures starlight deflection during a solar eclipse.

quote.text: Now I am happy that the theory is confirmed.

moments.takeaway: Gravity is geometry. Mass tells spacetime how to curve; curved spacetime tells matter how to move.

now.title: Gravity today
now.body:
General relativity passes every test we can throw at it: GPS satellites compensate for it nanosecond by nanosecond; LIGO detected gravitational waves from black hole mergers in 2015 (2017 Nobel Prize); the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of the M87 black hole in 2019.

We still don't have a quantum theory of gravity. General relativity and quantum mechanics are both extraordinarily successful, and incompatible at the deepest level.
now.open_questions: How does gravity emerge from a quantum-mechanical theory? What happens inside black holes? What is dark energy (responsible for the universe's accelerating expansion)? What is dark matter (which gravitates but doesn't shine)? Why is gravity so much weaker than the other fundamental forces?

items.reflection: Newton was extraordinarily reluctant to publish. His Principia, the most important book in physics, was written under duress from Halley. How much of the history of science depends on chance interventions by people willing to push a reluctant genius into print?

moments.title: Hertz notices a peculiar effect
moments.body:
Hertz is producing electromagnetic waves with a spark-gap transmitter to confirm Maxwell's prediction. He notices that ultraviolet light on the receiver electrodes makes sparks easier to produce.

He reports the effect in passing — 'I will not say it has no important consequences' — but moves on. He dies in 1894 at age 36 without pursuing it.
moments.takeaway: A small anomaly tucked into a paper. It becomes the seed of a revolution.

moments.title: Lenard's measurements
moments.body:
Lenard quantifies the photoelectric effect. Three results puzzle classical physics:
- The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends on the frequency of light, not its intensity.
- Below a threshold frequency, NO electrons are emitted regardless of how bright the light.
- Emission is essentially instantaneous (less than a nanosecond), even at very low intensity.

Classical wave theory predicts the opposite: intensity should set energy, and weak light should take a long time to build up enough energy to release an electron.
moments.takeaway: Light's particle-like behaviour starts to assert itself in measurements that wave theory cannot explain.

moments.title: Einstein's heuristic paper
moments.body:
Einstein, age 26, working as a patent clerk, publishes 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light'. He proposes light energy is concentrated in discrete quanta of energy E = hf.

His equation: K_max = hf - phi (phi being the work function). Frequency below phi/h gives no emission. Above threshold, K_max scales linearly with f. The numbers are testable.

quote.text: In accordance with the assumption to be considered here, the energy of a light ray spreading out from a point source is not continuously distributed over an increasing space, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta...

moments.takeaway: Light is quantised. The 'heuristic' word is Einstein hedging — most physicists think the idea is unphysical.

moments.title: Millikan's reluctant confirmation
moments.body:
Millikan spends 10 years trying to disprove Einstein's equation. He carefully measures K_max vs f for various metal surfaces and gets a perfect linear relationship, with slope h/e — Planck's constant divided by the electron charge — matching theory to within 1 percent.

Millikan accepts the equation but doesn't accept light quanta as physical realities. 'In spite of the apparently complete success' of Einstein's equation, 'the physical theory of which it was designed to be the symbolic expression is found so untenable that Einstein himself, I believe, no longer holds to it.'
moments.takeaway: Even decisive confirmation does not necessarily mean acceptance of the underlying picture.

moments.title: Einstein's Nobel Prize
moments.body:
Einstein wins the Nobel Prize 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' The Nobel Committee specifically does NOT mention relativity, which is still considered controversial.

The photoelectric effect remained Einstein's only experimentally tested theory at the time the prize was awarded.
moments.takeaway: Einstein's most famous work (relativity) is not what got him the Nobel. The photoelectric paper was the safest choice.

now.title: Photons today
now.body:
Single photons are routinely produced and detected. Quantum cryptography uses single-photon polarisation states for unbreakable key distribution (in principle). Photomultiplier tubes count individual photons; superconducting nanowire detectors achieve near 100 percent efficiency.

Quantum electrodynamics describes how photons interact with charged matter to ridiculous precision (the magnetic moment of the electron is predicted and measured to 12 significant figures).
now.open_questions: Can we ever 'see' the wavefunction of a single photon directly? How can quantum optics scale up to fully quantum computing networks? Is the photon truly a fundamental particle, or might it have substructure at energies beyond our reach?

items.reflection: Einstein's 1905 photon paper was his own most cited paper for decades. He later called the quantisation of light 'the only really revolutionary thing I have done' — even more than relativity. Yet most contemporaries took years to accept the picture. Why do specific revolutionary ideas struggle for acceptance even from people willing to use the equations?

moments.title: Slipher measures galaxy redshifts
moments.body:
Slipher (working alone, with old equipment) takes spectra of 'spiral nebulae' (now known to be other galaxies). Most are redshifted, suggesting they are moving away. By 1917 he has measurements for 25 of them.

What the spirals are — clouds in our galaxy, or distant 'island universes' — is still disputed.
moments.takeaway: The data are there, but the interpretation depends on knowing what spiral nebulae are.

moments.title: Hubble proves Andromeda is its own galaxy
moments.body:
Using the 100-inch Hooker Telescope (then the largest in the world), Hubble identifies Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula. Their period-luminosity relation (calibrated by Henrietta Leavitt in 1912) gives the distance: about 1 million light-years (we now know it's 2.5 million).

Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way. The universe is much bigger than anyone had supposed.
moments.takeaway: The Milky Way is not the universe. It's one of many galaxies.

moments.title: Lemaître proposes expansion from a singular point
moments.body:
Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, applies Einstein's field equations and proposes the universe is expanding from an initial 'primeval atom'. He derives a velocity-distance relation: v = H * d, two years before Hubble's empirical version.

Lemaître's paper is in French and in a small Belgian journal. Einstein dismisses the idea: 'Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.'
moments.takeaway: The Big Bang was proposed before Hubble's data forced the issue. Einstein resists for years.

moments.title: Hubble's law
moments.body:
Hubble publishes recession velocities (from Slipher's data) vs distances (his own measurements) for 24 galaxies. The relation is linear: v = H * d. Distance galaxies recede faster.

This is the canonical evidence for an expanding universe. Hubble himself was cautious about the interpretation — he sometimes preferred to say galaxies SEEM to recede.
moments.takeaway: The universe is expanding. The further away you look, the faster it's receding.

moments.title: Penzias and Wilson discover the cosmic microwave background
moments.who: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, Bell Labs, Holmdel
moments.body:
Penzias and Wilson are calibrating a horn antenna for radio astronomy. They detect a uniform 'noise' from all directions at about 3 Kelvin. They scrub the antenna for pigeon droppings — still there.

A nearby Princeton group (Dicke, Peebles, Roll, Wilkinson) had predicted exactly this: cooled-down photons from a hot Big Bang. The two groups publish back to back. Penzias and Wilson win the 1978 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The Big Bang's afterglow is detected by accident. Cosmology becomes a precision science.

now.title: Cosmology today
now.body:
The universe is 13.787 billion years old (Planck satellite, 2018). It contains about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter and 68 percent dark energy. The Cosmic Microwave Background is the most precisely measured electromagnetic spectrum in physics, agreeing with a blackbody at 2.7255 K to better than 1 part in 10,000.

JWST (launched 2021) is now imaging galaxies less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.
now.open_questions: What's dark matter? What's dark energy? Why is the universe so smooth at large scales (the horizon problem)? Inflation gives an explanation but raises new questions. What came before the Big Bang? Did the universe have a beginning, or has it always been? Are there multiple universes?

items.reflection: Lemaître proposed the expanding universe in 1927 — two years before Hubble's data — and proposed the Big Bang in 1931. Yet 'Hubble's law' bears Hubble's name, not Lemaître's. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union officially renamed it the Hubble-Lemaître law. How long does science wait to correct attribution, and what does the delay tell us about how we remember discovery?

moments.title: Rutherford classifies alpha and beta radiation
moments.body:
Rutherford, a New Zealander working at McGill in Montreal, distinguishes two kinds of radiation from uranium: alpha (heavy, slow, stopped by paper) and beta (light, fast, stopped by thin metal). Villard later adds gamma (the most penetrating).

Rutherford goes on to identify alpha particles as helium nuclei.
moments.takeaway: Radioactivity is sorted into types. Rutherford's career as 'the father of nuclear physics' is launched.

moments.title: Geiger and Marsden's startling backscatter
moments.who: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, Manchester
moments.body:
Working under Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fire alpha particles at gold foil. Most pass through with small deflections, consistent with the plum-pudding model. But about 1 in 8000 bounce nearly straight back.

In Rutherford's famous reaction: 'It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'
moments.takeaway: Backscatter is impossible if the atom's positive charge is spread out smoothly. Something dense and small must be deflecting the alphas.

moments.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
moments.body:
Rutherford proposes the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting at relatively huge distance. He calculates the nucleus must have a radius less than 10 to the minus 14 m — far smaller than the atom (10 to the minus 10 m).

Most of the atom is empty space. Atoms are mostly nothing.

quote.text: It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life.
quote.attrib: Ernest Rutherford, on the gold foil results

moments.takeaway: Atoms are mostly empty space. The plum pudding model dies.

moments.title: Chadwick discovers the neutron
moments.body:
Working under Rutherford, Chadwick is puzzled by a 'radiation' from beryllium bombarded by alpha particles. The radiation has no charge but knocks protons out of paraffin. Calculation: it must be a neutral particle of about the proton's mass.

Chadwick gets the Nobel Prize in 1935. The neutron explains why isotopes exist and underwrites the entire chemistry of nuclei.
moments.takeaway: The nucleus contains protons AND neutrons. The structure of matter is now mostly mapped out.

moments.title: Deep inelastic scattering — protons have parts
moments.body:
High-energy electrons fired at protons at SLAC scatter at sharper angles than a smooth proton would allow — exactly the same kind of evidence as Rutherford's gold foil, just at higher energy. The protons contain tiny pointlike scatterers.

These are quarks, predicted by Gell-Mann and Zweig in 1964. The Nobel-Prize-winning analysis (Friedman, Kendall, Taylor, 1990) confirms quark structure.
moments.takeaway: The pattern repeats. Rutherford's atomic substructure is mirrored at the next scale down.

now.title: Nuclear physics today
now.body:
We know about 3,000 isotopes of 118 elements. Nuclear reactors, medical isotopes, ion beam therapy and nuclear weapons all build on Rutherford's nuclear atom. Quark/gluon structure of nucleons is described by quantum chromodynamics — confirmed at the LHC and elsewhere.

The nuclear chart still has frontier regions: superheavy nuclei (elements 119 and beyond) and exotic neutron-rich nuclei produced at facilities like FRIB (Michigan).
now.open_questions: Where does the 'island of stability' for superheavy elements lie? What's the neutron-rich limit of stable nuclei? What happens inside neutron stars (giant atomic nuclei)? Can we image the internal structure of protons more directly?

items.reflection: Rutherford was a brilliant experimentalist and an opinionated administrator. He won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (despite being a physicist) and famously remarked: 'In science there is only physics; all the rest is stamp collecting.' How do disciplinary rivalries shape who claims which discoveries?

moments.title: Young's double slit
moments.body:
Newton had argued light was made of 'corpuscles'. Young presents a paper to the Royal Society showing that light passing through two narrow slits produces interference fringes — exactly what waves do, and what particles can't.

The paper is poorly received in Britain. Newton's authority is too great. The wave theory gains ground only after Fresnel develops it mathematically in the 1810s, and Foucault measures light speed in water (slower than in air, as waves should be — particles should be faster) in 1850.

quote.text: The supposition of waves... will explain a variety of phenomena which cannot easily be accounted for in any other way.

moments.takeaway: Light is waves. Newton was wrong. The wave model dominates for the next century.

moments.title: Taylor's faint-light interference
moments.body:
Taylor (a 23-year-old undergraduate) does an experiment to test whether interference is built up by individual photons. He photographs a diffraction pattern using light SO FAINT that on average only one photon is in the apparatus at a time.

Exposures take months. The interference pattern still forms. Each photon, individually, behaves wave-like.
moments.takeaway: Single particles interfere with themselves. Light is both wave and particle — and so are particles.

moments.title: Davisson and Germer — electrons diffract
moments.who: Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, Bell Labs
moments.body:
Davisson and Germer accidentally heat a nickel crystal during an electron-scattering experiment, creating a clean single-crystal surface. They get sharp diffraction peaks in the scattered electrons.

The electrons interfere as waves with wavelengths matching de Broglie's prediction (lambda = h/p, 1924). Matter has wave properties.
moments.takeaway: Particles diffract. The wave-particle duality is not a property of light alone.

moments.title: Tonomura's single-electron build-up
moments.body:
Tonomura's team builds an electron biprism — an electrostatic analogue of Young's slits — and fires single electrons one at a time at a detector screen. They record where each electron lands.

In early frames there's a scatter of dots, looking entirely random. After tens of thousands of electrons, the dots accumulate into a sharp interference fringe pattern. Each electron — alone in the apparatus, no other electrons to interfere with — contributes to a coherent fringe pattern.
moments.takeaway: The interference pattern is genuinely the behaviour of a single particle, NOT the result of many particles colliding.

moments.title: Molecules of 2000 atoms interfere
moments.body:
The Vienna group sends giant molecules (functionalised oligoporphyrins, ~25,000 amu, ~2000 atoms) through a Talbot-Lau interferometer. Interference fringes form.

This pushes the wave-particle duality up by orders of magnitude in mass. Where the line is between 'quantum object' and 'classical object' remains unclear — and the existing answer is 'we haven't found it yet'.
moments.takeaway: Quantum interference works for molecules of biological scale. There is no obvious upper limit to wave-particle duality.

now.title: Wave-particle duality today
now.body:
Quantum mechanics' formalism (wavefunctions in Hilbert space) makes wave-particle duality natural — particles and waves are not separate things but different aspects of one quantum state. Decoherence theory explains why everyday objects don't show interference: the environment 'measures' them constantly, collapsing superpositions.

Applications: electron microscopy (sub-Angstrom resolution), neutron diffraction (probing magnetism), matter-wave interferometry (precision sensors, atomic clocks).
now.open_questions: What sets the boundary between quantum and classical? Is decoherence sufficient, or is something else needed (objective collapse theories)? Can macroscopic objects (viruses, bacteria) be put into superposition states?

items.reflection: Young's 1801 result was correct, but contradicted Newton's authority and was suppressed in England for decades. Foreign chemists (Fresnel, Foucault) had to demonstrate it before British physics accepted it. How do scientific authority and national pride bias the acceptance of well-supported results?

moments.title: Three teams predict the Higgs mechanism
moments.who: Brout & Englert; Higgs; Guralnik, Hagen & Kibble
moments.body:
Three independent papers in 1964 — Englert and Brout (Brussels), Higgs (Edinburgh), Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble (Imperial College) — propose a mechanism that gives fundamental particles mass.

They postulate a field permeating all space; particles interact with it and acquire mass. Higgs (alone among the six authors) explicitly mentions a new boson as a consequence. The boson eventually bears his name.
moments.takeaway: The mechanism that gives particles mass is proposed by three groups in months — none of whom collaborated.

moments.title: Electroweak unification
moments.body:
Weinberg and Salam apply the Higgs mechanism to the electroweak theory of Glashow. The new theory unifies electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force, requires the Higgs boson, and predicts the W and Z bosons.

't Hooft and Veltman (1971) prove the theory is renormalizable — finite predictions are possible. The Nobel Prize follows for many of these names in 1979 (electroweak) and 1999 (renormalization).
moments.takeaway: The Higgs boson becomes a key prediction of the unified electroweak theory.

moments.title: W and Z bosons discovered at CERN
moments.body:
Carlo Rubbia leads the UA1 detector at CERN's SPS proton-antiproton collider. They detect the W and Z bosons at the predicted masses. The electroweak theory's mass-bearing particles are real.

The Higgs boson is the only major missing piece of the Standard Model. Its mass is not predicted by theory; only its existence is required.
moments.takeaway: The Standard Model is now mostly confirmed. The Higgs is the missing tile.

moments.title: Building the LHC
moments.body:
The Large Hadron Collider — a 27 km ring of superconducting magnets, 100 metres underground at CERN — is approved in 1994. Construction takes 14 years. The cost is about 4.75 billion Swiss francs.

Four main detectors: ATLAS, CMS, LHCb, ALICE. ATLAS and CMS are designed primarily to find the Higgs (or rule it out).
moments.takeaway: The largest scientific instrument ever built, for one specific question.

moments.title: Higgs discovery announcement
moments.body:
On 4 July 2012, CERN announces that both ATLAS and CMS have independently observed a new particle at mass 125 GeV with statistical significance over 5 sigma. The properties match the Higgs boson.

Peter Higgs and François Englert (Brout had died in 2011) win the 2013 Nobel Prize. Higgs commented that he had not really expected to live to see the discovery — he was 83.

quote.text: It is an incredible thing that it has happened in my lifetime.

moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction from 1964 is confirmed in 2012. Particle physics' Standard Model is complete.

now.title: Particle physics today
now.body:
The Standard Model — 17 fundamental particles, three forces (electromagnetic, weak, strong), the Higgs — describes everything we have measured at colliders. It has been tested to extraordinary precision.

The LHC continues. The High-Luminosity LHC upgrade aims to run through the 2030s. Plans for the next generation of colliders (FCC, ILC, muon collider) are being developed.
now.open_questions: What is dark matter? Why is gravity not in the Standard Model? Why are there exactly three generations of particles? Why is the Higgs mass so 'small' (hierarchy problem)? Where are the BSM (Beyond Standard Model) particles?

items.reflection: The Higgs discovery involved over 6,000 physicists on the two detectors and decades of work. Yet only three of the six original theorists could be awarded a Nobel (which limits laureates to three per prize). Brout had died; Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble were not honoured. How does science fairly assign credit to a discovery involving hundreds of theorists and thousands of experimentalists?

moments.title: Carnot's reflections
moments.body:
Sadi Carnot, 28 years old, publishes 'Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu'. He asks the question: what is the maximum efficiency of a heat engine?

He answers: an idealised cyclic engine operating between two temperatures (hot Th, cold Tc) has efficiency at most 1 - Tc/Th, regardless of the working substance. Any real engine does worse. The result holds even though Carnot is still working in the framework of the caloric theory (heat as a conserved fluid).
moments.takeaway: Even without correct theoretical foundations, Carnot deduces the central principle of heat engines.

moments.title: Carnot dies in obscurity
moments.body:
Carnot dies of cholera in the 1832 Paris epidemic at age 36. His personal effects, including notebooks, are burned for fear of contagion. His 1824 book had only sold 600 copies and was largely forgotten.

Clapeyron (1834) rediscovers and develops Carnot's ideas, putting them into mathematical form. They are taken up by Kelvin and Clausius in the 1840s and 1850s.
moments.takeaway: Almost the entire output of a foundational thinker is destroyed by a panicked health response.

moments.title: Clausius defines entropy
moments.body:
Clausius formalises Carnot's principle in terms of a new state function. He defines: change in entropy equals heat transferred divided by absolute temperature, dS = dQ/T (for reversible processes).

The second law of thermodynamics: entropy of an isolated system never decreases. In 1865 he gives entropy its name (from the Greek for 'transformation').

quote.text: Die Energie der Welt ist konstant; die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu. (The energy of the world is constant; the entropy of the world tends toward a maximum.)

moments.takeaway: Energy is conserved (first law); usable energy is not (second law). The arrow of time has a name.

moments.title: Boltzmann's statistical interpretation
moments.body:
Boltzmann shows that entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic configurations consistent with a given macroscopic state. S = k log W. Entropy increase is statistical inevitability — disordered configurations are vastly more numerous than ordered ones.

Boltzmann's interpretation reduces a phenomenological law to a counting argument. It also opens the door to statistical mechanics. The formula S = k log W is engraved on his grave.
moments.takeaway: Macroscopic thermodynamic laws emerge from microscopic statistics. Reductionism wins another round.

moments.title: Boltzmann's suicide
moments.body:
Boltzmann's atomistic and statistical interpretation of physics was bitterly opposed by Mach, Ostwald and the 'energeticists' who rejected atoms as unobservable speculation. Boltzmann suffered chronic depression.

On holiday in Duino in 1906, Boltzmann hanged himself. His wife and daughter found him. Within a few years atomism was definitively confirmed by Einstein's analysis of Brownian motion (1905) and Perrin's experiments. He didn't live to see it.
moments.takeaway: Boltzmann died before his interpretation was vindicated. He never knew he was right.

now.title: Thermodynamics today
now.body:
Thermodynamics is the most foundational physical theory we have — it survives every paradigm shift. Even quantum field theory and general relativity must satisfy thermodynamic laws.

Applications span every branch of science: refrigeration, internal combustion engines, biological metabolism, information theory (Shannon entropy is mathematically identical to Boltzmann's), black hole thermodynamics (Bekenstein, Hawking), the early universe.
now.open_questions: Why does the universe seem to have started in a low-entropy state? (We don't know.) Can we make engines that approach Carnot efficiency in practice? How does entropy relate to information in quantum systems? Is the third law (S → 0 as T → 0) really fundamental, or an artefact of how we define entropy?

items.reflection: Carnot died at 36 with his work unrecognised. Boltzmann killed himself a year before the atomistic worldview he championed was confirmed. Both founded thermodynamics; both lived in the shadow of resistance from their contemporaries. What does it say about science that its foundations were laid by people who didn't see their work accepted in their lifetimes?

moments.title: Ørsted's compass needle
moments.body:
Ørsted is giving a lecture on electricity and notices that a compass needle near a wire deflects when current flows through the wire. Electricity produces magnetism.

Within weeks, Ampère in Paris quantifies the effect. Within months, electromagnets begin replacing horseshoe magnets in laboratories.
moments.takeaway: Electricity and magnetism are connected. The two fields begin to fuse.

moments.title: Faraday's induction
moments.body:
Faraday discovers electromagnetic induction: moving a magnet near a wire induces a current. Changing magnetic flux drives electromotive force.

Faraday had no formal mathematical training. He thinks in terms of 'lines of force' filling space — a field. His ideas are dismissed as unmathematical by many of his contemporaries.

quote.text: The lines of force, then, are conditions of the surrounding space, and not particular lines.

moments.takeaway: Faraday's 'lines of force' become the modern concept of a field. Mathematical formalism comes later.

moments.title: Maxwell's equations
moments.body:
Maxwell formalises Faraday's intuition with four differential equations. They unify electricity, magnetism and (crucially) light: the equations predict electromagnetic waves travelling at exactly the speed of light, c.

Light is an electromagnetic wave.

quote.text: We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.

moments.takeaway: Three sciences (electricity, magnetism, optics) collapse into one theory.

moments.title: Hertz produces and detects radio waves
moments.body:
Hertz builds a spark-gap transmitter and a loop receiver. He generates electromagnetic waves at radio frequencies and detects them across a room. He measures their wavelength, polarisation and reflection — all consistent with Maxwell's predictions.

When asked about applications, Hertz says: 'It's of no use whatsoever ... we just have these mysterious electromagnetic waves that we cannot see with the naked eye. But they are there.'
moments.takeaway: Maxwell's prediction of electromagnetic waves is experimentally confirmed. Within 10 years Marconi has commercial radio.

now.title: Electromagnetism today
now.body:
Maxwell's equations underpin radio, television, mobile phones, GPS, microwaves, lasers, MRI, the entire electricity grid. They were one of the inputs to Einstein's special relativity. Their relativistic completion (Lorentz covariance) is automatic. Quantum electrodynamics (QED) extends them to the quantum regime with extraordinary precision.

Light has been used to compute (photonics), to communicate (optical fibres carry > 90 percent of long-distance data), and to manipulate matter (laser cooling, optical tweezers).
now.open_questions: Can we make better photonic computers? Can we generate and shape arbitrary quantum states of light? Are there modifications to QED at extreme energies or fields (axion-like particles, photon mass)?

items.reflection: Faraday was a bookbinder's apprentice with no mathematical education. His 'lines of force' were ignored by formal physicists for decades. Maxwell took Faraday's intuitive picture seriously and formalised it. Two contrasting modes of doing physics — intuitive geometry and rigorous mathematics — turn out to be deeply complementary. Which is more important to a scientist's success: pictures or formalism?

moments.title: Bell Labs invents the point-contact transistor
moments.who: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, William Shockley, Bell Labs
moments.body:
On 16 December 1947, Bardeen and Brattain demonstrate amplification of an audio signal through a point-contact transistor made of germanium. Bell Labs immediately recognises the significance.

Shockley, the team's manager, had been working on a related device. He produces his own (better) bipolar junction transistor within months.
moments.takeaway: The vacuum tube has a solid-state replacement: small, cool, low-power, robust. Electronics changes forever.

moments.title: Nobel Prize and the founding of Silicon Valley
moments.body:
The trio share the Nobel Prize in Physics. Shockley moves to California and founds Shockley Semiconductor in 1956. His management style drives away his best engineers.

The 'Traitorous Eight' (Noyce, Moore, Hoerni, Last, Kleiner, Roberts, Grinich, Blank) leave to start Fairchild Semiconductor in 1957. From Fairchild come Intel (Noyce and Moore, 1968), AMD, and a long lineage of silicon companies.
moments.takeaway: Shockley's bad management arguably founded Silicon Valley, by forcing his employees to start their own companies.

moments.title: Integrated circuit
moments.body:
Kilby and Noyce independently develop the integrated circuit: multiple components on a single semiconductor substrate. Kilby's design (germanium, hand-wired) is older. Noyce's (silicon, photolithographically patterned) is the practical winner.

Integrated circuits scale: 1965 sees Gordon Moore predict transistor count per chip will double every year (later revised to every two years). 'Moore's law' holds for roughly 50 years.
moments.takeaway: Integration enables exponential scaling. A single chip eventually carries billions of transistors.

moments.title: Intel 4004 — the first microprocessor
moments.body:
Intel releases the 4004, designed for a Japanese calculator company. It contains 2,300 transistors at 10 micrometre feature size, runs at 740 kHz, and performs about 92,000 operations per second.

This 'computer on a chip' makes personal computing possible. By 1981 the IBM PC ships with an Intel 8088 (29,000 transistors). By 2024 a single Apple M-series chip contains over 130 billion transistors at 3 nanometre feature size.
moments.takeaway: A general-purpose computing device fits on a fingernail. Information technology hands the world a new infrastructure.

now.title: Semiconductors today
now.body:
Modern chips integrate over 100 billion transistors on a single die. Smartphones contain compute power that would have filled a building in 1980. Semiconductors are the foundation of communications, computing, control systems, scientific instruments, medical devices, and AI.

Fundamental physics: band theory describes electron behaviour in periodic potentials; doping creates n-type and p-type regions; junctions enable transistors, diodes, photovoltaics, LEDs.
now.open_questions: Can Moore's law continue? (Feature size is approaching atomic limits.) What replaces silicon — gallium nitride, 2D materials like graphene, carbon nanotubes? Can quantum computers (using superconducting qubits, trapped ions, photonics) outperform classical for important problems?

items.reflection: Shockley's later career involved increasingly racist views and a falling-out with the scientific community. His Nobel and his ideas about race are sometimes presented as separate. Should the work of a great scientist be remembered separately from their public conduct?

moments.title: Onnes discovers superconductivity
moments.body:
Onnes had been the first to liquefy helium in 1908, reaching 4.2 K. He measures the resistance of mercury as it cools. At 4.2 K, the resistance drops suddenly to ZERO — unmeasurably low.

Mercury becomes a superconductor. Onnes wins the 1913 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Some materials lose all electrical resistance below a critical temperature. Mechanism unknown.

moments.title: Meissner effect
moments.who: Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld, Berlin
moments.body:
Meissner and Ochsenfeld discover that a superconductor doesn't merely allow current to flow without resistance — it actively expels magnetic fields from its interior. This is the Meissner effect: superconductors are PERFECT diamagnets.

This is more than 'zero resistance' (which would lock in any pre-existing field). It's a genuine new state of matter.
moments.takeaway: Superconductivity is a distinct thermodynamic phase — not just very-good conductivity.

moments.title: BCS theory
moments.who: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, University of Illinois
moments.body:
Bardeen (who had already won one Nobel for the transistor), Leon Cooper and J. Robert Schrieffer publish a microscopic theory of superconductivity. Electrons in a superconductor pair up ('Cooper pairs') via lattice vibrations and condense into a single quantum state.

The theory wins a 1972 Nobel — Bardeen's second. He is the only person to win two Nobel Prizes in Physics.
moments.takeaway: Superconductivity is a macroscopic quantum effect. Electrons cooperate via lattice vibrations to form pairs that flow without resistance.

moments.title: High-temperature superconductivity
moments.body:
BCS theory predicted a ceiling of about 30 K for superconductivity. Bednorz and Müller find ceramic copper oxides (cuprates) that superconduct at 35 K, then 90 K (above liquid nitrogen, 77 K) — vastly easier and cheaper to cool.

The 1987 Nobel comes a year after publication — fastest Nobel ever for a physics discovery. Mechanism is still not fully understood. Cuprates don't obey BCS theory cleanly.
moments.takeaway: A new class of superconductors works above the BCS ceiling. Theory is left behind by experiment.

moments.title: Hydride superconductors at near-room temperature, high pressure
moments.body:
Sulfur hydrides, lanthanum hydrides and other 'hydride' compounds show superconductivity above 200 K — but only at million-atmosphere pressures.

Claims of room-temperature superconductivity at lower pressures (carbonaceous sulfur hydride, 2020; LK-99, 2023) have been retracted or failed replication. The field is active, contested, and sometimes embarrassing.
moments.takeaway: Higher-temperature superconductors keep appearing — but practical room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductivity remains elusive.

now.title: Superconductors today
now.body:
Superconductors are used in MRI scanners, particle accelerators (LHC magnets), MagLev trains and high-precision instruments (SQUIDs). Quantum computers built on superconducting qubits (Google, IBM) leverage Cooper-pair physics directly.

The field still has fundamental mysteries: the cuprates' mechanism, the iron pnictides, the rich phenomenology of pairing symmetries.
now.open_questions: Is room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductivity possible? What's the mechanism in cuprates? Can we design superconductors using machine learning + computation? What new states of matter lurk near the superconducting transition?

items.reflection: John Bardeen is the only person to win two Nobel Prizes in Physics — for the transistor and for BCS theory. He was famously low-key, even shy. How does a single person produce two field-defining works? And why did Marie Curie (the only person with Nobels in two different sciences) win such different recognition for it?

moments.title: Halley asks Newton a question
moments.who: Edmund Halley visits Isaac Newton, Cambridge
moments.body:
Halley, Wren and Hooke have been arguing in London whether an inverse-square gravitational force could produce Kepler's elliptical orbits. None of them can do the maths. Halley travels to Cambridge in August 1684 to ask Newton.

Newton replies casually that he had worked it out years ago and the orbits would be ellipses, but had mislaid the proof. He promises to redo and send it.
moments.takeaway: A casual conversation triggered the writing of the most important book in physics.

moments.title: Principia Mathematica published
moments.body:
Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica appears in July 1687, funded by Halley out of his own pocket because the Royal Society had spent its budget on a fish atlas. It is written in Latin.

The book contains the three laws of motion, the universal law of gravitation (F = G m1 m2 / r²), and demonstrations that Kepler's laws follow from gravity acting on planets. It also shows that comets follow conic-section orbits — including the prediction (verified after Halley's death) that the 1682 comet would return.

quote.text: Hypotheses non fingo. (I frame no hypotheses.)
quote.attrib: Isaac Newton, General Scholium added to the Principia's second edition

moments.takeaway: Mechanics becomes a quantitative, predictive science. Physics has its founding text.

moments.title: Opticks
moments.body:
Newton publishes Opticks (in English, not Latin), summarising decades of work on light and colour. He shows white light is a mixture of colours by splitting it with a prism and recombining it; he argues light is corpuscular (particles); he proposes a particulate theory of refraction.

The wave theory of light (Huygens, Young, Fresnel) will eventually displace Newton's corpuscles in the 19th century — only to return in modified form as photons in the 20th.
moments.takeaway: Newton's authority shapes optics for over a century, partly correctly, partly slowing acceptance of wave theory.

moments.title: Newton dies, buried at Westminster Abbey
moments.body:
Newton dies at age 84 having served as Master of the Royal Mint (where he viciously prosecuted counterfeiters) and President of the Royal Society. He is buried in Westminster Abbey with state honours — the first scientist so honoured.

Voltaire, present at the funeral, was astonished: 'He was buried like a king who had done well by his subjects.' Voltaire helped popularise Newtonianism in France through his Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733).
moments.takeaway: Newton becomes the model of the scientist-as-national-hero. His name dominates physics for two centuries.

now.title: Newtonian mechanics today
now.body:
Newton's laws are still the working tools of almost all engineering and most physics below relativistic and quantum scales. Spacecraft trajectories, structural mechanics, fluid dynamics, planetary motion — all are computed with Newton.

General relativity (1915) supersedes Newton at very high speeds, very strong gravity, or very large scales. Quantum mechanics (1925-1926) supersedes Newton at atomic scales. Both reduce to Newton in their respective classical limits.
now.open_questions: Can we unify general relativity and quantum mechanics — both built on different foundations from Newton's — into a quantum theory of gravity? What is dark matter (which gravitates Newtonian-style but doesn't shine)? What is dark energy (which gravitates 'wrong')?

items.reflection: Newton was reluctant to publish. The Principia was extracted from him by Halley's persistence and funded out of Halley's own pocket. How much of the history of physics depends on chance interventions by people willing to push reluctant geniuses into print?

moments.title: Galvani's frog legs
moments.body:
Galvani is dissecting frogs and notices that their legs twitch when touched simultaneously by two different metals. He concludes the legs contain 'animal electricity' — a vital fluid intrinsic to the tissue.

His colleague Alessandro Volta disagrees. He argues the electricity comes from the dissimilar metals in contact with the moist tissue, not from anything biological.
moments.takeaway: A scientific disagreement frames the next decade of work. Volta sets out to prove the electricity is non-biological in origin.

moments.title: Volta builds the voltaic pile
moments.body:
Volta announces in a letter to the Royal Society of London a 'pile' of alternating zinc and silver discs, separated by cardboard soaked in brine. The pile produces a steady electric current — the first continuous electrical source in history.

Letter dated 20 March 1800. The Royal Society's president, Joseph Banks, reads it out and arranges publication. Within months, scientists across Europe are building larger piles and discovering new chemistry.

quote.text: I have at last constructed an apparatus which... gives the same shocks as the Leyden jar, charged to but a feeble degree, but which without any previous charge gives a shock continuously and incessantly.
quote.attrib: Alessandro Volta, letter to Sir Joseph Banks, 1800

moments.takeaway: Electricity is no longer transient sparks from rubbing or storage in Leyden jars — it flows continuously from a chemical source.

moments.title: Nicholson, Carlisle and Davy split water and isolate new metals
moments.body:
Nicholson and Carlisle (London, May 1800) use a voltaic pile to electrolyse water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. The chemistry of water is no longer mysterious.

Humphry Davy (London, 1807-1808) uses much larger voltaic piles to isolate sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, barium and strontium for the first time. The pile opens up half of inorganic chemistry within a decade.
moments.takeaway: A new technology — continuous current — transforms chemistry. Whole branches of inorganic chemistry suddenly become possible.

moments.title: The volt is named
moments.body:
The unit of electric potential difference is named the volt in his honour at the 1881 International Electrical Congress. Volta had died in 1827.

The same congress names the ampere (Ampère), the ohm (Ohm), the coulomb (Coulomb), and the farad (Faraday). The pantheon of early electrical pioneers is enshrined in the SI.
moments.takeaway: The fundamental units of electricity are named after the people who made the subject possible.

now.title: Batteries today
now.body:
Lithium-ion batteries (developed by Whittingham 1976, Goodenough 1980, Yoshino 1985 — 2019 Nobel Prize) now power phones, laptops, electric cars and grid storage. Energy densities approach 300 Wh/kg.

Lead-acid (cars), nickel-metal-hydride (older hybrids), zinc-air (hearing aids) and many other chemistries exist. Solid-state batteries (no liquid electrolyte) are under intense development.
now.open_questions: Can battery energy density approach the gravimetric limit of about 5 kWh/kg set by Li-air or sulfur chemistry? Can production scale to meet electric vehicle and grid demands without unsustainable rare-element mining? Can recycling reach the 95+ percent recovery needed for a circular battery economy?

items.reflection: Galvani thought he had found a vital force; Volta proved him wrong. Both were partly right: nerves do work by electrical signalling, and Volta's pile generates current from chemistry, not biology. How often is a scientific dispute resolved by both parties being partly right, only to be remembered as a winner-takes-all?

moments.title: Ørsted finds magnetism from current
moments.body:
Ørsted, lecturing on electricity, notices that a compass needle near a wire deflects when current flows through the wire. Electric current produces a magnetic field. Within months, Ampère in Paris quantifies the effect.

The symmetric question is open: can a magnetic field produce a current? Many try; none succeed. Faraday, an apprentice bookbinder turned chemist at the Royal Institution, takes up the problem.
moments.takeaway: Half the connection between electricity and magnetism is established. The other half is a 11-year puzzle.

moments.title: Faraday's induction
moments.body:
On 29 August 1831 Faraday wraps two coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring. Connecting one to a battery, he notices a brief deflection in a galvanometer on the other coil — but only when the battery is switched on or off, not while current flows steadily.

The insight: it's the CHANGE in magnetic flux that induces EMF, not the flux itself. Within months he demonstrates that moving a magnet in and out of a coil produces alternating current.

quote.text: I have had an electric eel.
quote.attrib: Michael Faraday, in another diary entry — but in 1831 he simply writes: 'The current sets in the contrary direction when the conjunction with the battery is broken.'

moments.takeaway: Changing magnetic flux drives EMF. The principle of every dynamo, transformer and motor is born.

moments.title: Lines of force become a field
moments.body:
Faraday has almost no mathematical training. He visualises electromagnetic phenomena as 'lines of force' filling space — invisible but real. He sprinkles iron filings on paper above a magnet and sees the lines made visible. He pictures the field, not action-at-a-distance, as the medium of force.

Most mathematicians of his era dismiss the picture as unrigorous. Maxwell will take it seriously.

quote.text: The lines of force, then, are conditions of the surrounding space, and not particular lines.
quote.attrib: Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, Vol. III

moments.takeaway: Faraday invents the concept of a field. Mathematics catches up to him 30 years later.

moments.title: Maxwell mathematises Faraday's intuition
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' in 1865. He puts Faraday's lines of force into four differential equations governing electric and magnetic fields.

The equations predict electromagnetic waves travelling at exactly the speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave. Faraday's intuition, given mathematical form, unifies electromagnetism and optics.
moments.takeaway: Faraday's pictures and Maxwell's equations are the same physics, in different languages.

now.title: Induction today
now.body:
Faraday's induction underpins every motor, generator, transformer, induction cooker and wireless phone charger. World electric grids depend on it.

Induction is also the principle behind eddy-current braking (used in trains, roller coasters and laboratory dampers) and inductive heating (used in metallurgy and welding).
now.open_questions: Can wireless power transfer scale up to charge vehicles in motion on roads, and to charge implanted medical devices for life? Can superconducting motors and generators (which exploit zero ohmic loss) replace conventional machines economically?

items.reflection: Faraday left school at 13 and worked as a bookbinder's apprentice. He had no university degree. He became Director of the Royal Institution, gave the Christmas Lectures for decades, and changed physics. How does science deal with self-taught outsiders compared with formally trained insiders?

moments.title: Maxwell formalises Faraday's field
moments.body:
Maxwell, in his late twenties, sets out to mathematise Faraday's lines of force. Over a decade he develops the field equations governing electric and magnetic phenomena. He adds a crucial new term — the displacement current — to make the equations self-consistent.

With the displacement current in, the equations have wave solutions.
moments.takeaway: Adding a missing term to make the equations consistent gives them wave solutions automatically.

moments.title: Maxwell predicts light is electromagnetic
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society. The equations predict electromagnetic waves travel at speed c = 1 / √(μ0 ε0) — calculated from electric and magnetic constants measured in static lab experiments.

The result is exactly the measured speed of light. Maxwell concludes: 'We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.'

quote.text: We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.
quote.attrib: James Clerk Maxwell, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, 1865

moments.takeaway: Three sciences — electricity, magnetism, optics — collapse into one theory. Light is an electromagnetic wave.

moments.title: Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes a two-volume treatise systematising the field. In the original notation it had 20 equations. Heaviside (in the 1880s) reformulates the system using modern vector calculus into the familiar four equations we now call 'Maxwell's equations'.

The four-equation form is what we teach today. Maxwell died young (cancer, 1879, age 48) and never saw his electromagnetic wave prediction experimentally confirmed.
moments.takeaway: The grand synthesis of 19th-century physics. Two volumes that defined the next century's electromagnetism.

moments.title: Hertz produces and detects radio waves
moments.body:
Hertz builds a spark-gap transmitter and a loop receiver. He generates electromagnetic waves at radio frequencies (about 30 MHz) and detects them across a room. He measures wavelength, polarisation and reflection — all consistent with Maxwell.

When asked about applications, Hertz says he sees none — 'It's of no use whatsoever... we just have these mysterious electromagnetic waves that we cannot see with the naked eye. But they are there.' Marconi will commercialise radio within 10 years.
moments.takeaway: Maxwell's prediction is experimentally confirmed in his absence. Radio waves are real.

now.title: Maxwell's equations today
now.body:
Maxwell's equations underpin radio, television, mobile phones, GPS, microwaves, lasers, MRI, the electricity grid and the entire optical-fibre internet backbone. They were one of the inputs to Einstein's special relativity (1905). Their relativistic completion is automatic.

Quantum electrodynamics (QED, Feynman, Schwinger, Tomonaga, Dyson — 1965 Nobel) extends Maxwell's equations to the quantum regime. QED is the most precisely tested theory in physics — the electron's magnetic moment is predicted and measured to about 12 decimal places.
now.open_questions: Can we generate and shape arbitrary quantum states of light? Are there modifications to QED at extreme energies or in extreme fields (e.g. photon-photon scattering observed at the LHC in 2017)? Could axion-like particles or a non-zero photon mass be detected in precision experiments?

items.reflection: Maxwell's equations predicted electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths but he only knew about light. Every part of the spectrum we now use (radio, microwaves, X-rays, gamma rays) was discovered after his death. How often does a theory predict more than its creators can imagine?

moments.title: Maxwell predicts electromagnetic waves
moments.body:
Maxwell's equations predict that any oscillating electric current must produce electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light. The prediction sits as theoretical speculation for 23 years.

Maxwell dies in 1879. The waves are still hypothetical.
moments.takeaway: A bold theoretical prediction sits unconfirmed for over two decades.

moments.title: Hertz sets up the apparatus
moments.body:
Hertz, then 30, builds a transmitter: a Ruhmkorff induction coil driving an oscillating spark between two brass spheres separated by a small gap. The spark creates rapidly oscillating currents — and so, by Maxwell, electromagnetic waves.

His receiver is a simple wire loop with a small spark gap. When waves from the transmitter reach the loop, a tiny spark jumps the receiver gap. Hertz can darken the room to see it more easily.
moments.takeaway: An elegant apparatus reduces the question to one observable: do tiny sparks appear at the receiver?

moments.title: Hertz detects, measures, characterises
moments.body:
Hertz systematically maps the waves: he measures their wavelength (around 4 metres for his apparatus), shows they reflect off metal sheets, refract through pitch prisms, polarise through grids of parallel wires, and produce standing-wave patterns by interference. All the optical properties Maxwell's theory predicts.

He publishes 14 papers in 1888. Maxwell's prediction is fully confirmed.

quote.text: It's of no use whatsoever... we just have these mysterious electromagnetic waves that we cannot see with the naked eye. But they are there.
quote.attrib: Heinrich Hertz, on being asked the practical value of his work

moments.takeaway: Electromagnetic waves are real. They behave optically. They can be generated and detected in the lab.

moments.title: Marconi commercialises radio
moments.body:
Within seven years of Hertz's death (1894), Marconi has built up the basic technology to commercial scale: long-distance wireless telegraphy. By 1901 he transmits the letter 'S' across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

Marconi wins the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. Hertz (who died young of an infection at 36) is honoured posthumously: the unit of frequency, the hertz, is named for him in 1930.
moments.takeaway: Pure physics becomes a global communication infrastructure within a generation.

now.title: The electromagnetic spectrum today
now.body:
The electromagnetic spectrum — radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays — is all one phenomenon, differing only in wavelength. The full spectrum spans more than 20 orders of magnitude. Mobile phones use ~1 GHz; FM radio ~100 MHz; Wi-Fi ~2.4 GHz or ~5 GHz; 5G up to ~30 GHz; medical X-rays ~10 to the 18 Hz.

Global telecommunications, broadcasting, navigation (GPS), remote sensing (weather radar, satellite imagery), heating (microwave ovens), and astronomy (radio telescopes through gamma-ray observatories) all use parts of the spectrum.
now.open_questions: Can higher-frequency parts of the spectrum (terahertz, mm-wave) be exploited for next-generation wireless networks? Can quantum-mechanical control of single radio-frequency photons (quantum radio) become useful?

items.reflection: Hertz was confident his discovery had no practical applications. Within a generation, radio reshaped global communication. How often do scientists drastically misjudge the future impact of their work — and what does this tell us about funding 'curiosity-driven' research?

moments.title: Becquerel and the cloudy day
moments.body:
Becquerel had been testing whether phosphorescent uranium salts emit penetrating rays after sunlight exposure. Cloudy weather forces him to put the experiment in a drawer with the unexposed plates. He develops them anyway. They are exposed.

Uranium emits its own penetrating radiation, without any sunlight involvement. He has discovered what Marie Curie will later name 'radioactivity'.
moments.takeaway: Some elements spontaneously emit penetrating radiation. Discovered by accident in a Paris drawer.

moments.title: The Curies isolate two new elements
moments.body:
Marie Curie picks up Becquerel's work for her PhD. Using a sensitive electrometer designed by Pierre and Jacques Curie, she measures radioactivity quantitatively in many samples. She finds pitchblende (uranium ore) more radioactive than its uranium content alone explains.

Over four years in a leaky shed, the Curies process tonnes of pitchblende and isolate first polonium (July 1898, named for Poland), then radium (December 1898).

quote.text: Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood.

moments.takeaway: Two new highly radioactive elements isolated by hand in a shed. The link between chemistry and nuclear physics is now firmly established.

moments.title: First Nobel Prize in Physics
moments.body:
The Curies share the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Becquerel. The Committee initially names only Becquerel and Pierre. Pierre writes refusing the prize unless Marie is included. She becomes the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

They are too ill from radiation exposure to travel to Stockholm.
moments.takeaway: Formal recognition of radioactivity — and of a woman as a Nobel laureate for the first time.

moments.title: Second Nobel — Chemistry
moments.body:
Pierre died in 1906 (run over by a horse-drawn cart). Marie continues alone. In 1911 she wins a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for her isolation of pure radium metal.

She is still the only person ever to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. The same year, the French Academy of Sciences denies her election by a single vote — because she is a woman, foreign, and recently scandalised by a press attack on her relationship with the physicist Paul Langevin.
moments.takeaway: Recognition is uneven even at the highest level. Two Nobels, but no Academy seat.

now.title: Radioactivity today
now.body:
Radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) is understood as a quantum-mechanical process governed by the weak and strong nuclear forces. About 3000 isotopes of 118 elements are catalogued. Many are made artificially in reactors and accelerators.

Applications include medical imaging (PET, SPECT), therapy (cobalt-60, iodine-131), dating (carbon-14, uranium-lead), industrial gauging, and (controversially) nuclear power and weapons.
now.open_questions: Why do certain magic numbers of protons or neutrons make nuclei especially stable? Where is the predicted 'island of stability' for superheavy elements? How safely can long-lived nuclear waste be managed over geological time?

items.reflection: Marie Curie died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, almost certainly from her decades of radiation exposure. Her notebooks are still so radioactive they are kept in lead boxes and require protective equipment to handle. What does it say about the cost of discovery that an entire family — Marie, Pierre, Irène, Frédéric — all died of radiation-related disease?

moments.title: Photoelectric paper
moments.body:
Einstein, 26 years old and working as a junior patent clerk in the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, publishes 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light' in Annalen der Physik (received 18 March 1905). He proposes light energy comes in discrete quanta of size hf.

The equation K_max = hf - φ predicts the photoelectric effect's frequency-dependent threshold. This is the paper that wins him the 1921 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: Light is quantised — particles of energy hf. The 'heuristic' label is Einstein's hedge: he knew most physicists would find the idea unphysical.

moments.title: Brownian motion paper
moments.body:
'On the Motion of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid, as Required by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat' (received 11 May). Einstein derives the statistics of the random jiggling of pollen grains observed by Brown in 1827 from molecular collisions.

The analysis gives Avogadro's number from the measurable mean-square displacement of suspended particles. Perrin's 1908-1909 experiments confirm it. Atoms are real, measurable objects — not just bookkeeping conveniences.
moments.takeaway: Atomic theory acquires direct experimental support. Mach's anti-atomist philosophy collapses.

moments.title: Special relativity
moments.body:
'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies' (received 30 June). Einstein resolves the long-standing puzzle that Maxwell's equations look different in different inertial frames. He postulates: (1) the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames; (2) the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames.

From these two postulates, he derives time dilation, length contraction, the loss of simultaneity, and the relativistic addition of velocities. Newtonian mechanics is shown to be an approximation valid only at low speeds.

quote.text: It is known that Maxwell's electrodynamics — as usually understood at the present time — when applied to moving bodies, leads to asymmetries which do not appear to be inherent in the phenomena.
quote.attrib: Albert Einstein, opening sentence of the 1905 special relativity paper

moments.takeaway: Space and time are not absolute. Einstein, at the patent office, has rewritten Newtonian mechanics.

moments.title: E = mc squared
moments.body:
'Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?' — a three-page follow-up to the special relativity paper (received 27 September). Einstein derives that any body losing energy ΔE must lose mass ΔE/c² as well.

In modern form: E = mc². The result is later confirmed by nuclear physics — the binding energy of nuclei equals the mass defect times c². The same equation underlies nuclear weapons and stellar fusion.
moments.takeaway: Mass and energy are interchangeable. The fourth of Einstein's 1905 papers contains arguably his most famous equation.

now.title: Einstein's legacy today
now.body:
Special relativity is part of the daily workings of GPS satellites (their clocks must be corrected for time dilation), particle accelerators (energies far above mc²), and high-precision atomic clocks.

The photoelectric effect underpins solar panels, photomultiplier tubes, and digital cameras (CCDs). Brownian motion analysis underpins modern statistical mechanics and stochastic-process modelling in finance, biology and chemistry. E = mc² is engineered routinely in fusion-research reactors, medical-isotope production, and (more grimly) nuclear weapons.

Einstein went on to general relativity (1915), the photon-statistics work that led to lasers (Bose-Einstein, 1924), and the famous EPR critique (1935) that became the test bed for Bell's theorem.
now.open_questions: Can general relativity be reconciled with quantum mechanics? Why is the speed of light exactly what it is? Could variations in physical constants over cosmological time be detected by precision measurement?

items.reflection: Einstein in 1905 was 26, was not a university professor, had no PhD when he started writing the papers (he submitted his Brownian motion paper as his doctoral thesis at Zurich the same year), and was working at a patent office. Four foundational papers in a single year. How does this happen — and how often do we systematically miss similar outsiders today?

moments.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
moments.body:
Rutherford proposes (1911) the nuclear atom: a tiny dense positive nucleus surrounded by electrons at relatively huge distances. The model has a problem: classical electromagnetism predicts orbiting electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus within nanoseconds. Atoms shouldn't exist at all.

Niels Bohr arrives in Manchester from Denmark in 1912 and takes up the problem.
moments.takeaway: The Rutherford atom is unstable by classical physics. Something new is needed.

moments.title: Bohr's three-part paper
moments.body:
Bohr publishes three papers in the Philosophical Magazine. He proposes:
(1) Electrons in atoms can occupy only specific 'stationary' orbits with quantised angular momentum (n × h-bar).
(2) Electrons in these orbits do NOT radiate, classical electromagnetism notwithstanding.
(3) When an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one, a photon of frequency f = (E1 - E2)/h is emitted.

The model reproduces the Rydberg formula for hydrogen's emission spectrum exactly: 1/λ = R(1/n1² - 1/n2²), with R = 1.097 × 10 to the 7 per metre.

quote.text: How wonderful that we have met with a paradox. Now we have some hope of making progress.

moments.takeaway: Quantisation is in. Hydrogen's spectrum is explained quantitatively. The classical picture of orbits is on borrowed time.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body:
Bohr wins the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms and of the radiation emanating from them'. He is 37.

The Bohr model is celebrated as the first quantum theory of an atom. It also has obvious limitations: it works for hydrogen but not for helium or anything heavier. The exclusion principle, electron spin, and ultimately the full quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Schrödinger and Dirac will be needed to handle the rest.
moments.takeaway: Bohr's model is a partial answer that is still recognisable in today's chemistry teaching of 'shells' and 'energy levels'.

moments.title: Bohr's institute, the Copenhagen interpretation
moments.body:
Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen becomes the hub of quantum physics. Heisenberg works there in 1924-1927 developing matrix mechanics; Pauli is a frequent visitor; Schrödinger writes wave mechanics in Zurich but Bohr engages it deeply.

The 'Copenhagen interpretation' of quantum mechanics — measurement, complementarity, wave-particle duality — comes out of these years. Einstein's famous disagreement with Bohr (the EPR paper, 1935) plays out in correspondence and at conferences for decades.
moments.takeaway: Quantum physics' philosophical framework is developed in Copenhagen. Bohr is its presiding architect.

now.title: Atomic structure today
now.body:
We now describe atoms by the Schrödinger equation: electrons occupy orbitals (s, p, d, f) — probability distributions, not classical orbits. The Pauli exclusion principle, spin, and many-electron interactions explain shell filling and the periodic table.

Bohr's 1913 model survives as a teaching simplification. It correctly captures discrete energy levels, the formula for hydrogen's spectrum, and the emission/absorption of photons by quantum jumps — but it's the wrong picture for any atom beyond hydrogen.
now.open_questions: Can quantum chemistry from first principles reach computational chemistry's accuracy for arbitrary molecules? How do quantum effects play out in biological macromolecules at body temperature?

items.reflection: Bohr's 1913 model worked perfectly for hydrogen but completely failed for helium. The right answer for one atom and complete failure for the next — that's a strong signal that the model captures something deep but is also missing something deeper. How should physics deal with theories that are partly brilliant and partly wrong?

moments.title: Heisenberg invents matrix mechanics
moments.body:
Heisenberg, suffering from hay fever, retreats to the rocky North Sea island of Helgoland to recover. There he writes the foundational paper of matrix mechanics. He represents physical observables (position, momentum, energy) by infinite matrices that don't commute: xp - px = i h-bar.

The paper is mailed to Max Born in Göttingen, who recognises the matrices for what they are and rapidly develops them with Pascual Jordan into a full theory.
moments.takeaway: A completely new mathematical framework for atomic physics emerges on a wind-swept island.

moments.title: Schrödinger writes the wave equation
moments.body:
Schrödinger publishes his wave equation in Annalen der Physik. The equation iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Hψ governs the time evolution of a wavefunction ψ.

Solving for hydrogen gives orbitals (s, p, d, f) — probability distributions, not classical orbits — and the correct hydrogen spectrum. Within months Schrödinger shows his wave mechanics and Heisenberg's matrix mechanics are mathematically equivalent.

quote.text: I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it.
quote.attrib: Erwin Schrödinger, later, on the probabilistic interpretation of his own equation

moments.takeaway: Two completely different-looking formulations of quantum mechanics turn out to describe the same physics.

moments.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
moments.body:
Heisenberg proposes the uncertainty principle: Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2. Position and momentum cannot both be simultaneously well-defined. The result follows mathematically from the non-commuting matrix mechanics.

Bohr extends this to a general principle of complementarity: wave and particle pictures are mutually exclusive but jointly necessary descriptions of quantum systems.
moments.takeaway: Uncertainty is structural, not just a measurement limitation. The very concepts of position and momentum are limited.

moments.title: Nobel Prizes
moments.body:
Heisenberg wins the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded retrospectively in 1933 'for the creation of quantum mechanics'. Schrödinger and Dirac share the 1933 Nobel 'for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory'.

Born's contribution (he provided the probabilistic interpretation of the wavefunction in 1926, |ψ|² = probability density) is not honoured until 1954.
moments.takeaway: Three foundational physicists honoured almost simultaneously. The new mechanics has arrived.

now.title: Quantum mechanics today
now.body:
Quantum mechanics is the most precisely tested theory in physics. Every prediction has been confirmed where measurable. It underpins atomic, molecular, nuclear, solid-state, particle and quantum-information physics.

Applications: lasers, transistors, MRI, atomic clocks, GPS, every photonic and electronic device, quantum cryptography (commercial), quantum computers (under construction). The 2022 Nobel Prize for Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger honoured Bell-test experiments — confirming that nature really is non-classical.
now.open_questions: What does measurement actually do physically? Why does the quantum-to-classical transition happen and where does it sit? Can practical quantum computers solve classically hard problems at scale? Is there a deeper layer beneath quantum mechanics?

items.reflection: Schrödinger came to hate the probabilistic interpretation of his own equation. Einstein hated quantum mechanics for decades ('God does not play dice'). The founders' philosophical discomfort with their own theory has not been fully resolved a century later. How should physics treat a theory that is empirically perfect but conceptually disputed?

moments.title: Slipher measures galactic redshifts
moments.body:
Slipher, working alone with comparatively modest equipment, takes spectra of 'spiral nebulae' (later understood to be other galaxies). Most show redshifted spectra — they are moving away from us. By 1917 he has 25 such measurements.

Whether the spirals are inside our galaxy or far outside is still disputed. Without distances, Slipher's redshifts cannot be interpreted as cosmological recession.
moments.takeaway: The data are gathered before they can be understood. Slipher's redshifts will become the cosmological foundation 12 years later.

moments.title: Hubble proves Andromeda is a separate galaxy
moments.body:
Hubble identifies Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda nebula using the 100-inch Hooker Telescope (then the largest in the world). Cepheids' period-luminosity relation (calibrated by Henrietta Leavitt in 1912) gives the distance — about 1 million light-years.

Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way. The 'spirals' are other galaxies. The universe is vastly bigger than anyone had assumed.
moments.takeaway: The Milky Way is not the universe. It's one galaxy among hundreds of billions.

moments.title: Lemaître proposes the expanding universe
moments.body:
Georges Lemaître, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, applies Einstein's general relativity to the universe as a whole. He derives that the universe must be expanding from an initial 'primeval atom'. He even derives a velocity-distance relation: v = H × d.

The paper is in French in a small Belgian journal. Einstein responds: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable.' (Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.)
moments.takeaway: The Big Bang is proposed before Hubble's data forces the issue. Einstein resists for years.

moments.title: Hubble's law
moments.body:
Hubble plots recession velocities (mostly from Slipher's measurements) against distances (his own measurements using Cepheids) for 24 galaxies. The relation is linear: v = H × d, with H about 500 km/s per megaparsec (modern value is about 70).

Hubble himself is cautious about the cosmological interpretation. He sometimes prefers to say galaxies 'apparently recede'. But the data are the canonical evidence for an expanding universe.
moments.takeaway: Empirically, the universe is expanding. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to recede.

moments.title: Hubble-Lemaître law
moments.body: The IAU votes to rename 'Hubble's law' as the 'Hubble-Lemaître law', recognising Lemaître's prior derivation. Lemaître had been quietly ignored or forgotten for decades; the rename is an acknowledgement that scientific attribution sometimes needs correction.
moments.takeaway: Names of laws can be officially corrected — though it takes most of a century.

now.title: Cosmology today
now.body:
The universe is 13.787 billion years old (Planck satellite, 2018). It contains about 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter, 68 percent dark energy. The Cosmic Microwave Background (discovered 1964, precision-measured by COBE/WMAP/Planck) is the most precisely characterised electromagnetic spectrum in physics.

JWST (launched 2021) is now imaging galaxies less than 300 million years after the Big Bang. The Hubble constant H0 is currently measured by different methods to ~67 km/s/Mpc (CMB-based) vs ~73 km/s/Mpc (local distance ladder) — the 'Hubble tension' remains an open puzzle.
now.open_questions: What is dark matter? What is dark energy? What resolved the Hubble tension between early-universe and late-universe measurements? What happened before the Big Bang? Did time itself begin then?

items.reflection: Lemaître published the expanding universe in 1927 in French — and was ignored. Hubble published the same in 1929 in English with more data — and got a law named after him for nearly a century. How do language, geography and academic networks shape who gets credit in science?

moments.title: Dirac equation
moments.body:
Dirac writes down a relativistic wave equation for the electron. The equation automatically incorporates spin and predicts the existence of antimatter — the positron, discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932.

The equation has infinities. Calculations of small corrections (like the electron's anomalous magnetic moment) diverge to infinity. Quantum electrodynamics is born but plagued by infinities for two decades.
moments.takeaway: Relativistic quantum theory exists but doesn't yet compute finite answers.

moments.title: Shelter Island Conference
moments.body:
A small conference at Shelter Island brings together America's leading physicists to discuss postwar problems in physics. Two new precision measurements force the issue: the Lamb shift (Willis Lamb's measurement of a tiny shift in hydrogen energy levels) and the electron's anomalous magnetic moment (Rabi's group).

Both need a theory that can calculate finite results from QED.
moments.takeaway: The experimental challenge is laid. Theory must respond.

moments.title: Renormalisation by three independent paths
moments.body:
Three independent formulations of renormalisable QED appear within months. Tomonaga (Tokyo) and Schwinger (Harvard) use canonical methods. Feynman (Cornell) develops his sum-over-histories formulation and the famous diagrams.

Freeman Dyson (Cornell, then IAS) shows the three formulations are equivalent. The infinities can be systematically absorbed into renormalised mass and charge, leaving finite predictions.
moments.takeaway: QED becomes computable. Three independent paths to the same theory — a sign that the theory is robust.

moments.title: Feynman diagrams enter physics
moments.body:
Feynman's diagrams — pictures of particles propagating and interacting at vertices — provide an intuitive bookkeeping for QED calculations. Every diagram corresponds to a mathematical contribution to the scattering amplitude.

The diagrams become the universal language of particle physics. They are adopted, with extensions, for QCD, electroweak theory, and ultimately the Standard Model.
moments.takeaway: A pictorial calculus replaces pages of algebra. Particle physics has its visual vocabulary.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body:
The 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics is shared by Tomonaga, Schwinger and Feynman for QED. Dyson is not included — limited to three laureates per prize. Feynman gives an iconic Nobel lecture.
