QED becomes the template for all subsequent quantum field theories.
moments.takeaway: Three nationalities, three independent solutions to the same problem, all honoured together.

now.title: QED today
now.body:
QED is the most precisely tested theory in physics. The electron's anomalous magnetic moment (g-2) is predicted by QED and measured experimentally to about 12 significant figures — agreement is essentially perfect. (A small experimental-theoretical tension in muon g-2 is currently the subject of intense investigation.)

QED is the working model for all interactions of charged particles with light. It is also the model for how quantum field theories should be constructed — and was extended to QCD (the strong force) and electroweak theory.
now.open_questions: What's the source of the muon g-2 discrepancy? Are there particles or interactions beyond the Standard Model contributing to the precision tests of QED? Why are the fine-structure and other constants what they are?

items.reflection: Three physicists in three countries reached the same theory at nearly the same time after WWII. Tomonaga worked in war-damaged Tokyo with food rationing; Schwinger in Harvard; Feynman in Cornell. Independent simultaneous discovery often signals that an idea's time has arrived. How does science account for the role of historical timing in discovery?

moments.title: Einstein predicts gravitational waves
moments.body:
Einstein, having completed general relativity in November 1915, predicts in 1916 that accelerating masses should produce ripples in spacetime — gravitational waves — travelling at the speed of light.

The predicted amplitudes are tiny. Einstein himself is sceptical that they could ever be detected. In 1936 he writes a paper (with Nathan Rosen) arguing they don't really exist — gets it rejected by Physical Review after peer review (he had never previously been peer-reviewed and was furious) and eventually withdraws.
moments.takeaway: A core prediction of general relativity — that Einstein himself sometimes doubted — waits a century for confirmation.

moments.title: Binary pulsar PSR B1913+16
moments.who: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor, Arecibo
moments.body:
Hulse and Taylor discover a pulsar in a binary system with another neutron star. Over years of observation, they measure the orbital period shortening at a rate exactly matching the prediction of gravitational-wave emission carrying energy away from the system.

This is the first indirect detection of gravitational waves. The 1993 Nobel Prize is awarded.
moments.takeaway: Gravitational waves are real. Their energy loss can be measured indirectly through orbital decay.

moments.title: Building LIGO
moments.who: LIGO collaboration, Hanford and Livingston, USA
moments.body:
The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory consists of two L-shaped detectors, each with arms 4 km long, in Hanford (Washington) and Livingston (Louisiana). Laser light bounces between mirrors at the ends of the arms. Passing gravitational waves stretch and squeeze the arms by tiny amounts (less than 10 to the minus 18 m).

Construction starts in 1994. First operations 2002. After 13 years of upgrades and null results, Advanced LIGO begins observing on 18 September 2015.
moments.takeaway: An instrument sensitive enough to measure a fraction of a proton's diameter over 4 kilometres. The most precise length measurement humans have built.

moments.title: GW150914 — first direct detection
moments.body:
At 09:50:45 UTC on 14 September 2015 — just days after Advanced LIGO begins observation — both detectors record a chirp signal lasting 0.2 seconds. The waveform matches predicted general-relativity gravitational waves from the merger of two black holes, 36 and 29 solar masses, into a single 62 solar mass black hole, about 1.3 billion light-years away.

Three solar masses' worth of energy is radiated as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second — briefly outshining all the stars in the observable universe.

quote.text: We have detected gravitational waves. We did it.
quote.attrib: David Reitze, LIGO Executive Director, press conference 11 February 2016

moments.takeaway: Einstein's 1916 prediction is confirmed exactly 100 years later. A new astronomy begins.

moments.title: Multi-messenger astronomy: GW170817
moments.body:
On 17 August 2017, LIGO and the Virgo detector in Italy observe gravitational waves from a neutron-star merger. Within 2 seconds, the Fermi space telescope detects a short gamma-ray burst from the same direction.

Within hours, optical telescopes worldwide point at the source and observe a 'kilonova' explosion. Heavy elements (gold, platinum, uranium) are observed being created in real time by r-process nucleosynthesis. The cosmic origin of half the elements heavier than iron is identified.
moments.takeaway: Gravitational waves, gamma rays, X-rays, optical, infrared and radio observations of the same event. Multi-messenger astronomy is born.

now.title: Gravitational-wave astronomy today
now.body:
Over 90 gravitational-wave events have been detected since 2015 — mostly binary black hole mergers, some neutron star mergers, one black hole-neutron star coalescence. The catalogue is growing every observing run.

LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA (Japan) operate. Future detectors: LISA (space-based, three spacecraft in formation, ESA/NASA, planned launch 2035) and Einstein Telescope (underground, Europe).
now.open_questions: What's the maximum mass of a black hole formed by stellar collapse? Do intermediate-mass black holes exist? Are there gravitational-wave sources beyond compact binaries (e.g. cosmic strings, primordial black holes)? Can we use gravitational waves to measure cosmological parameters independently of electromagnetic methods?

items.reflection: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916, doubted them in 1936, and was vindicated in 2015 — 60 years after his death. How does a discipline handle the gap between prediction and verification when it spans an entire human lifetime?

moments.title: Dalton revives the atom
moments.body:
A self-taught Quaker schoolmaster in Manchester publishes 'A New System of Chemical Philosophy'. He argues that each element is made of identical, indestructible atoms with characteristic weights, and that compounds form in whole-number ratios.

Dalton uses circle symbols with internal dots and bars to represent atoms. His own measurements of atomic weight are often wrong by a factor of two — but the framework is right.
moments.takeaway: After 2,000 years of Greek speculation, the atom becomes a quantitative scientific object.

moments.title: Thomson finds the electron
moments.who: J. J. Thomson, Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge
moments.body:
Thomson studies cathode rays. He shows the rays bend in electric and magnetic fields, calculates their charge-to-mass ratio, and finds it 1,800 times smaller than any atom.

He proposes the 'plum pudding' model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded inside. The atom, supposedly indivisible, has parts.
moments.takeaway: The first subatomic particle is discovered — and the atom is no longer indivisible.

moments.title: Rutherford's nucleus
moments.who: Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger, Ernest Marsden, Manchester
moments.body:
Geiger and Marsden fire alpha particles at thin gold foil. To everyone's astonishment, a small fraction bounce almost straight back.

Rutherford concludes nearly all the atom's mass is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus.

quote.text: It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.

moments.takeaway: The atom is mostly empty space, with a nucleus 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself.

moments.title: Bohr quantises the atom
moments.body:
Bohr proposes that electrons orbit only at fixed energy levels and jump between them by absorbing or emitting photons. He derives the hydrogen spectrum exactly.

Classical physicists are appalled — orbiting electrons should radiate and spiral in. But Bohr's predictions match experiment to four decimal places.
moments.takeaway: Quantisation enters the atom. Classical physics no longer applies inside it.

moments.title: Chadwick finds the neutron
moments.body:
Bothe and Becker in Germany find a mysterious neutral radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha particles. The Joliot-Curies think it is gamma rays.

Chadwick, in three frantic weeks, shows it must be a neutral particle with mass close to the proton — the neutron. Within years it will enable nuclear fission.
moments.takeaway: The atom's third major particle completes the picture — and opens the nuclear age.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Bohr model is taught at school but superseded by quantum mechanics. Scanning tunnelling microscopes now image individual atoms; the LHC probes structure 10^-19 m across.
now.open_questions: Why do fundamental constants have the values they do? Why three generations of matter?

items.reflection: Each model of the atom was 'wrong' but useful. When should you discard a model versus extend it?

moments.title: Faraday's ring experiment
moments.body:
A blacksmith's son with no university education wraps two coils of wire around opposite sides of an iron ring. Connecting and disconnecting one circuit makes a galvanometer needle in the other twitch.

A changing magnetic field induces a current. He repeats it with a copper disc rotating between magnet poles — the first electric generator.

quote.text: I have been busy again on Electro-Magnetic Induction and have got hold I think of a good thing.

moments.takeaway: Electricity from magnetism — the principle behind every power station today.

moments.title: Lenz's law
moments.body: Lenz states the direction rule: induced currents always oppose the change that produced them. The rule is a statement of energy conservation.
moments.takeaway: Conservation of energy makes induction a one-way street.

moments.title: Maxwell mathematises induction
moments.body: Maxwell writes induction as a partial differential equation. Combined with three others, it gives the complete classical theory of electromagnetism, predicting that fields propagate at the speed of light.
moments.takeaway: Faraday's intuitions become four lines of algebra describing all classical electromagnetism.

moments.title: Edison opens Pearl Street
moments.body: Edison opens the world's first central power station on Pearl Street, Manhattan. By 1893, Westinghouse and Tesla's AC system — which needs induction transformers — wins the 'War of Currents'.
moments.takeaway: Induction makes long-distance electricity transmission possible.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Faraday's law underpins generators, transformers, induction motors, induction hobs, wireless charging, MRI scanners and credit-card readers. About 99% of the world's electricity is generated by spinning a coil in a magnetic field.
now.open_questions: Can high-temperature superconducting cables transform the grid?

items.reflection: Faraday had almost no maths. Maxwell turned his images into equations. Was Faraday's lack of training a hindrance or an asset?

moments.title: Planck's reluctant quantum
moments.body:
Classical physics predicts a hot object should radiate infinite energy at high frequencies — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'. Planck, a 42-year-old conservative professor, derives a formula matching experiment perfectly.

To make it work he assumes energy is exchanged in discrete packets, E = hf. He calls h a 'mathematical trick' and spends years trying to remove it.

quote.text: It was an act of desperation. I had to obtain a positive result, under any circumstances and at whatever cost.

moments.takeaway: The quantum is born — as a calculation device the inventor does not believe in.

moments.title: Einstein takes the quantum seriously
moments.body: Einstein, 26, explains the photoelectric effect by assuming light itself comes in quanta — photons — each with energy hf. The paper is initially dismissed.
moments.takeaway: Light is both wave and particle. Einstein wins the 1921 Nobel for this paper, not for relativity.

moments.title: de Broglie's matter waves
moments.body:
A French aristocrat proposes the converse: if light waves are particles, matter particles are waves. Wavelength lambda = h/p.

The examiners are baffled. Langevin sends a copy to Einstein, who replies it is 'no madman's work'. Davisson and Germer confirm electron diffraction in 1927.
moments.takeaway: Wave-particle duality is universal.

moments.title: Solvay Conference
moments.who: Bohr, Einstein, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Born, Dirac, Pauli, Curie
moments.body: Seventeen of 29 attendees will win Nobel Prizes. Einstein and Bohr debate quantum mechanics in the corridors. Einstein: 'God does not play dice.' Bohr: 'Stop telling God what to do.'
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics works, even though no one fully agrees on what it means.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Quantum mechanics underlies transistors, lasers, MRI, GPS, and the entire semiconductor industry. Quantum computers reach hundreds of qubits in the 2020s.
now.open_questions: Is the wave function real or a tool? What collapses it?

items.reflection: Planck didn't believe in his own quantum. Einstein didn't believe in the implications. Why is a theory's creator often the wrong person to interpret it?

moments.title: Michelson-Morley find no ether
moments.body: Light supposedly travels through a luminiferous ether. They build a precision interferometer to detect Earth's motion through it. The expected fringe shift is 0.4; the observed shift is essentially zero.
moments.takeaway: Light has the same speed in every direction, no matter how you move.

moments.title: Einstein's relativity paper
moments.body: A 26-year-old Swiss patent clerk publishes 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies'. He assumes the speed of light is the same for all observers and derives time dilation and length contraction. He cites no one. Three months later he adds a four-page addendum: E = mc^2.
moments.takeaway: Space and time fuse into spacetime. Mass and energy fuse into one quantity.

moments.title: Minkowski's spacetime
moments.body: Einstein's old maths teacher (who once called him a 'lazy dog') gives relativity its geometric form. Spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold; the interval between events is invariant.

quote.text: Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows.

moments.takeaway: Spacetime is one object. The geometry comes first; everything else follows.

moments.title: Hafele-Keating clocks
moments.body: Atomic clocks flown around the world on commercial airliners return with measurably different elapsed times from a reference clock, confirming relativistic time dilation. Cost: about $8,000, mostly for tickets.
moments.takeaway: Time dilation is real. Every GPS satellite must correct for it.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Special relativity is the framework for all of high-energy physics. Particle accelerators reach 0.99999...c. GPS applies 38 microseconds/day of relativistic correction.
now.open_questions: Is Lorentz invariance exact, or does it break near the Planck scale?

items.reflection: Einstein had no lab and few equations beyond high-school algebra in 1905. What enabled his breakthrough that hundreds of better-equipped physicists missed?

moments.title: Einstein's 'happiest thought'
moments.body: Einstein has 'the happiest thought of my life': a person in free fall feels no gravity. Locally, acceleration and gravity are indistinguishable. This is the equivalence principle. He spends eight years learning differential geometry from his friend Marcel Grossmann.
moments.takeaway: Gravity is not a force — it is the geometry of spacetime.

moments.title: The field equations
moments.body: In November 1915, Einstein presents the field equations to the Prussian Academy. Days earlier, Hilbert had derived them independently. The equations predict Mercury's perihelion precession of 43 arcseconds per century beyond Newton — exactly the observed anomaly.
moments.takeaway: A century-old astronomical puzzle is solved by pure geometry.

moments.title: Eddington's eclipse
moments.body: An English Quaker pacifist leads expeditions to measure starlight bending around the eclipsed Sun. The prediction: 1.75 arcseconds (twice Newton's value). Eddington announces confirmation in November. Einstein becomes the first celebrity scientist.

quote.text: Lights All Askew in the Heavens; Men of Science More or Less Agog Over Results.

moments.takeaway: A British expedition validates a German Jewish theory months after war ends.

moments.title: Photographing a black hole
moments.body: The EHT, a planet-scale array of radio telescopes, releases the first image of the shadow of a black hole — M87*. The ring matches Einstein's prediction. In 2022 they image Sagittarius A* at the centre of our own galaxy.
moments.takeaway: A century after Einstein, we can photograph spacetime curvature.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: GR is tested to 1 part in 10^15 in some regimes. It underpins GPS, gravitational lensing surveys, and gravitational-wave astronomy. LIGO has detected ~100 mergers since 2015. But GR is incompatible with quantum mechanics.
now.open_questions: How is gravity quantised? What happens at singularities? Is spacetime emergent?

items.reflection: Einstein replaced Newton's universal force with curved geometry. When does a paradigm shift?

moments.title: Becquerel's cloudy week
moments.body: Investigating phosphorescence, Becquerel wraps uranium salts with photographic plates and plans to expose them to sunlight. Paris is overcast; the plates sit in a drawer for a week. He develops them anyway and finds clear images. The uranium emits its own penetrating radiation without sunlight.
moments.takeaway: A cloudy week in Paris launches the nuclear age.

moments.title: Marie and Pierre isolate polonium and radium
moments.body: Marie Skłodowska-Curie processes tonnes of pitchblende by hand in a leaky shed. She isolates polonium (named for her native Poland) and radium. She coins 'radioactivity'. She wins two Nobel Prizes (1903 Physics, 1911 Chemistry) — still the only person to win in two sciences.
moments.takeaway: Curie names a new branch of physics and gives it its instruments.

moments.title: Rutherford's alpha, beta, gamma
moments.body: Rutherford shows radioactive emissions come in three kinds: alpha (positive), beta (electrons), gamma (electromagnetic). In 1903 he and Soddy show radioactivity transmutes one element into another — the alchemists' dream, in reverse.
moments.takeaway: The atom can transform itself. Elements are not eternal.

moments.title: Curie's death
moments.body: Marie Curie dies of aplastic anaemia from decades of radiation exposure. Her notebooks remain radioactive a century later. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie has just discovered artificial radioactivity (1934 Nobel).
moments.takeaway: Curie pays with her life for the science she invented.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Radioactive decay underpins radiometric dating, medical imaging (PET, SPECT), cancer treatment, nuclear power and weapons. Tc-99m is used in 40 million medical procedures annually.
now.open_questions: Can spent nuclear fuel be safely stored for 10,000+ years?

items.reflection: Marie Curie handled radium with her bare hands. How should scientists balance discovery with caution about unknown risks?

moments.title: Fermi's uranium puzzle
moments.body: Fermi bombards uranium with neutrons and finds what he thinks are 'transuranic' elements heavier than uranium. The Italian press declares: 'Fermi creates new element 93!' In fact Fermi is splitting uranium atoms. He doesn't realise.
moments.takeaway: The most important nuclear discovery of the century happens — and is misidentified.

moments.title: Hahn, Meitner and fission
moments.who: Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner, Fritz Strassmann
moments.body:
Meitner, a Jewish Austrian physicist, has fled Nazi Germany to Sweden. Her collaborator Hahn writes describing a baffling result: uranium plus neutrons yields barium.

Walking in the snow with her nephew Otto Frisch on Christmas Eve, Meitner sees it: the uranium nucleus has split, releasing ~200 MeV. Hahn wins the 1944 Nobel alone; Meitner is omitted.
moments.takeaway: Fission is discovered in a winter forest, by a refugee theorist. The discoverer gets no Nobel.

moments.title: Szilárd's letter, signed by Einstein
moments.body: Hungarian refugee Szilárd drafts a letter to President Roosevelt warning of the possibility of a uranium bomb. He persuades Einstein to sign. The letter triggers the Manhattan Project. Szilárd later regrets it deeply.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical physicists initiate the most consequential weapons programme in history.

moments.title: Chicago Pile-1
moments.body:
Beneath the stands of a disused football stadium, Fermi's team assembles a pile of graphite and uranium. On 2 December 1942, control rods are withdrawn and the first self-sustaining chain reaction runs for 28 minutes.

A coded message: 'The Italian navigator has landed in the new world. The natives were friendly.'
moments.takeaway: The first nuclear reactor runs in a Chicago squash court.

moments.title: Trinity and Hiroshima
moments.body: On 16 July 1945, the Trinity test in New Mexico releases energy equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Three weeks later, Hiroshima and Nagasaki are destroyed; at least 110,000 people die immediately. Oppenheimer later recalls: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.'
moments.takeaway: Within seven years of fission's discovery, two cities are obliterated.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: About 440 nuclear reactors supply ~10% of global electricity. ITER aims for net fusion gain by 2035; NIF achieved scientific breakeven in 2022. Some 12,500 nuclear warheads remain in arsenals.
now.open_questions: Can fusion be made practical? Will the world abolish nuclear weapons before they are used again?

items.reflection: Meitner's contribution was excluded from the Nobel. Why does science still struggle to credit collaborators fairly?

moments.title: Particle zoo
moments.body: Post-WWII experiments discover dozens of new particles: pions, kaons, lambdas, sigmas. Wolfgang Pauli quips: 'Had I foreseen this, I would have gone into botany.'
moments.takeaway: Discovery outpaces theory. Order is desperately needed.

moments.title: Gell-Mann and Zweig propose quarks
moments.who: Murray Gell-Mann, Caltech; George Zweig, CERN
moments.body: Gell-Mann (who names them 'quarks' from Joyce's Finnegans Wake) and Zweig independently propose hadrons are built from three particles with fractional charge. The theory predicts the omega-minus, which is duly discovered. Zweig's paper is rejected; Gell-Mann wins the 1969 Nobel alone.

quote.text: Three quarks for Muster Mark!
quote.attrib: Joyce, Finnegans Wake — source of the name

moments.takeaway: Mathematical patterns predict particles before they are found.

moments.title: Deep inelastic scattering at SLAC
moments.body: At SLAC, high-energy electrons fired at protons bounce off at large angles — exactly as Rutherford's alphas bounced off gold nuclei. The proton has internal structure. Feynman calls the components 'partons'; they are quarks.
moments.takeaway: Rutherford's experiment, at a billion times the energy, reveals the proton's quark structure.

moments.title: Top quark at Fermilab
moments.body: The Tevatron discovers the top quark, completing the standard model's quark sector. Its mass, 173 GeV, is as heavy as a gold atom — astonishing for a fundamental particle.
moments.takeaway: All six quarks confirmed. The standard model is one of the most successful theories in physics history.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The standard model has 17 fundamental particles plus the Higgs. The LHC produces top quarks and Higgs bosons routinely. But the SM says nothing about dark matter, dark energy or gravity, and cannot explain neutrino mass.
now.open_questions: Why three generations? Why these mass values? Is there a deeper theory?

items.reflection: Gell-Mann initially called quarks a 'mathematical fiction'. When does a useful fiction become a real entity?

moments.title: Galileo's law of inertia
moments.body: Under house arrest after Inquisition condemnation, Galileo publishes 'Discourses on Two New Sciences' (smuggled to a Dutch publisher). He argues an object in motion will continue moving uniformly unless acted on — inertia. Aristotle had said motion requires constant force.
moments.takeaway: Without Galileo, no Newton. The first law of motion is born under house arrest.

moments.title: Principia Mathematica
moments.body: Newton's 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy', funded by Halley, sets out three laws of motion. The Principia unifies celestial and terrestrial mechanics.

quote.text: Hypotheses non fingo.

moments.takeaway: The most influential book in the history of science.

moments.title: Lagrange's reformulation
moments.body: Lagrange publishes 'Mécanique Analytique', proudly noting it contains no diagrams. He reformulates Newton's laws using one principle — minimisation of action — and a single function, the Lagrangian L = T - V.
moments.takeaway: Newton's three laws become one principle of least action.

moments.title: Hamilton's mechanics
moments.body: Hamilton reformulates mechanics again, using position and momentum as independent variables. The Hamiltonian H = T + V gives equations of motion as first-order differential equations. This formulation will be the natural setting for quantum mechanics.
moments.takeaway: A 19th-century reformulation prepares the way for 20th-century physics.

moments.title: Noether's theorem
moments.body: Noether — barred from a salaried position because she is a woman — proves a fundamental theorem: every continuous symmetry gives a conservation law. Time symmetry → energy. Space symmetry → momentum. Einstein calls it 'penetrating mathematical thinking'.
moments.takeaway: Conservation laws are not accidents — they are consequences of symmetry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Newton's laws still describe rockets, bridges, billiards. NASA trajectories to Pluto use them. Quantum and relativity correct Newton, but his framework operates in 99% of human-scale applications.
now.open_questions: Why are conservation laws so universal? What underlies symmetry itself?

items.reflection: Newton's mechanics 'works' but isn't fundamentally true. When is a theory good enough to use but wrong as a description of reality?

moments.title: Ibn Sahl's law of refraction
moments.body:
A Persian mathematician at the court of Caliph al-Sabi states the law of refraction (equivalent to modern n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2) in his work on burning mirrors and lenses. The manuscript will be forgotten for a thousand years.

Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in 1021 will write the Book of Optics, founding modern vision science.
moments.takeaway: The 'Snell' law is first written in 10th-century Baghdad. The history of physics is older and more global than the textbooks say.

moments.title: Snell rediscovers refraction
moments.body: Snellius rediscovers the law of refraction; he does not publish. Descartes publishes the same law in 1637, deriving it from a flawed argument that light travels faster in denser media. Fermat in 1657 derives it correctly from the principle of least time.
moments.takeaway: Three Europeans independently rediscover what Ibn Sahl found seven centuries earlier.

moments.title: Newton's prism
moments.body: Newton passes sunlight through a prism, then a second prism, and shows white light is composed of colours. He builds the first reflecting telescope, eliminating chromatic aberration. Robert Hooke disputes the work for decades.
moments.takeaway: White light is a mixture, not a pure substance.

moments.title: Young's double slit
moments.body: Thomas Young — physician, linguist (deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs), polymath — passes light through two narrow slits and shows it produces an interference pattern. Light is a wave. Newton's defenders attack him viciously.
moments.takeaway: A doctor with a sideline in linguistics demonstrates the wave nature of light.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Snell's law underlies every camera, telescope, microscope, fibre optic, and eye prescription. Modern optics has produced lasers, optical computing, integrated photonics and quantum communication. Fibre optic cables span ocean floors and carry essentially all internet traffic.
now.open_questions: Can we build optical computers competitive with electronic ones?

items.reflection: Why is the same law attributed to Snell rather than Ibn Sahl? Does naming reflect discovery, or power?

moments.title: Doppler in Prague
moments.body: An Austrian physicist proposes that the colour of stars shifts depending on their motion towards or away from us. He uses this to (incorrectly) explain binary star colours. The colour idea is wrong; the principle is right.
moments.takeaway: A flawed application of a profound principle.

moments.title: Trumpeters on a train
moments.body: Dutch meteorologist Buys Ballot tests Doppler's theory by putting a group of trumpeters on an open railway carriage and listening to the pitch shift as they pass. The shift is audible and matches Doppler's prediction.
moments.takeaway: One of the most charming confirmations in physics history.

moments.title: Cosmological redshift
moments.body: Hubble's discovery that galaxies recede with speed proportional to distance is the Doppler effect applied to cosmology. Doppler's principle goes from acoustic curiosity to cosmological diagnostic.
moments.takeaway: Doppler's modest acoustic effect becomes the key to the universe's expansion.

moments.title: First exoplanet by Doppler
moments.body: Mayor and Queloz detect 51 Pegasi b — the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star — by measuring tiny Doppler wobbles of the star induced by its planet. They win the 2019 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Doppler's principle locates planets around other stars.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Doppler effect is in police speed guns, weather radar, echocardiograms, GPS, and radio astronomy. Gravitational redshift, a relativistic cousin, is detected daily by GPS satellites.
now.open_questions: Can precision Doppler shifts detect Earth-like exoplanets in the habitable zone of Sun-like stars?

items.reflection: Doppler's original explanation was wrong. Yet he gets the prize and the law. When should a wrong application of a right idea be credited?

moments.title: Maxwell predicts waves
moments.body: Maxwell's equations imply oscillating charges should radiate electromagnetic waves at the speed of light. Light itself is one such wave, but the spectrum should extend far beyond visible frequencies.
moments.takeaway: The electromagnetic spectrum is predicted before any non-visible frequencies are seen.

moments.title: Hertz generates and detects radio
moments.body: Hertz builds a spark-gap transmitter and a wire loop receiver. He generates electromagnetic waves on one side of his lab and detects them across the room — the first man-made radio waves. Asked about applications, he replies: 'I do not think the wireless waves I have discovered will have any practical application.'

quote.text: It's of no use whatsoever... this is just an experiment that proves Maestro Maxwell was right.

moments.takeaway: Hertz confirms Maxwell — and famously misjudges the consequences.

moments.title: Marconi's transatlantic signal
moments.body: A 21-year-old Italian uses Hertz's apparatus to send wireless signals first across his garden, then across the English Channel (1899), and finally across the Atlantic (1901) — the letter 'S' from Cornwall to Newfoundland. Marconi wins the 1909 Nobel jointly with Karl Braun.
moments.takeaway: Within 14 years of Hertz's 'useless' discovery, the world has wireless telegraphy.

moments.title: Jansky and cosmic radio
moments.body: Jansky, investigating transatlantic radio interference, identifies a steady hiss coming from the Milky Way. He has discovered radio astronomy. The field will reveal pulsars, quasars, the CMB, and now allow us to image black holes.
moments.takeaway: Engineering noise turns out to be cosmic signal.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Radio waves underpin radio, TV, mobile phones, WiFi, Bluetooth, GPS, radar, MRI, microwave ovens, satellite communications and radio astronomy. About 50 billion connected devices now use the spectrum.
now.open_questions: Can 6G/THz wireless be made practical?

items.reflection: Hertz called his discovery useless. How often do scientists wrongly predict the impact of their work?

moments.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa
moments.body: Galileo allegedly drops a cannonball and a musket ball from the top of the Leaning Tower of Pisa. They land at the same time, contradicting Aristotle's claim that heavier objects fall faster. There is no contemporary record; it was reported by Galileo's student Viviani decades later. Galileo certainly did the experiment on inclined planes.
moments.takeaway: Whether or not it happened, the Pisa demonstration captures the death of Aristotelian physics.

moments.title: Inclined plane experiments
moments.body: Galileo rolls bronze balls down polished wooden inclines, measuring distances and times. He finds distance is proportional to time squared — uniform acceleration. He uses his pulse and a water clock for timing.
moments.takeaway: Modern physics begins with patient measurement, not philosophical argument.

moments.title: Two New Sciences
moments.body: Smuggled to a Dutch publisher, Galileo's last book presents his complete mechanics. He shows projectile motion is parabolic — the composition of horizontal motion with vertical acceleration. This is the first textbook of mathematical physics.
moments.takeaway: Under house arrest, Galileo founds modern mechanics.

moments.title: Hammer and feather on the Moon
moments.body: Astronaut Dave Scott drops a geological hammer and a falcon feather on the lunar surface. With no air, they hit the dust simultaneously — Galileo vindicated, 333 years after his death, on another world.
moments.takeaway: Galileo's claim is finally tested in a true vacuum — on the Moon.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The equivalence principle has been tested to 1 part in 10^15 by the MICROSCOPE satellite (2017). Lunar laser ranging tests it for the Earth and Moon falling around the Sun.
now.open_questions: Does the equivalence principle hold for quantum particles?

items.reflection: Galileo's inclined plane experiments were tedious; the tower story is what we remember. Why do we prefer dramatic myths to slow truth?

moments.title: Hertzsprung and Russell plot stars
moments.body: Hertzsprung in 1905-07 and Russell in 1913 plot stars on a diagram with temperature on one axis and luminosity on the other. Most stars fall on a diagonal 'main sequence'. Outliers are giants and dwarfs.
moments.takeaway: A simple scatter plot reveals the entire life cycle of stars.

moments.title: Payne and stellar composition
moments.body: Cecilia Payne, in her PhD thesis, applies Saha's ionisation theory to stellar spectra and concludes stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium — not iron, as everyone thought. Russell tells her the result is 'clearly impossible' and she must add caveats. Four years later he reaches the same conclusion and is widely credited.
moments.takeaway: A 25-year-old woman solves stellar composition — and is overridden by her male advisor.

moments.title: Chandrasekhar limit
moments.who: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, on a boat to England
moments.body: On the steamship from Madras to England, 19-year-old Chandrasekhar calculates that a white dwarf cannot exceed about 1.4 solar masses without collapsing. At Cambridge, Arthur Eddington publicly ridicules the result. Chandrasekhar receives the Nobel 53 years later, in 1983.
moments.takeaway: The most important stellar limit in astrophysics, derived on a steamship voyage.

moments.title: B^2FH paper
moments.who: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, Fowler, Hoyle
moments.body: The 'B^2FH' paper shows how every element heavier than helium is synthesised inside stars and supernovae. Carbon, iron, gold — all forged in stellar nucleosynthesis. Fowler wins the 1983 Nobel; Hoyle, who coined the term 'Big Bang' (originally as mockery), is omitted.

quote.text: We are made of star stuff.

moments.takeaway: Atoms in your body were forged inside dying stars.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Gaia (ESA) has mapped 1.8 billion stars in 3D. JWST resolves stellar populations across cosmic time. The Sun will leave the main sequence in ~5 billion years and become a red giant, then a white dwarf.
now.open_questions: What is the supernova explosion mechanism?

items.reflection: Cecilia Payne's correct result was dismissed by her senior male colleagues. How does science correct such errors?

moments.title: Schwarzschild solves Einstein's equations
moments.body:
Schwarzschild, a German artillery officer on the Russian front, solves Einstein's field equations for a spherical mass — just weeks after Einstein published them. He sends the solution to Einstein from a field hospital where he is suffering from pemphigus.

At a critical radius r = 2GM/c^2, something strange happens. Schwarzschild dies five months later.
moments.takeaway: The first solution to general relativity is derived on a battlefield. The author dies before its implications are understood.

moments.title: Oppenheimer and Snyder
moments.who: J. Robert Oppenheimer, Hartland Snyder, Berkeley
moments.body: Oppenheimer and his student show that a sufficiently massive collapsing star will collapse 'continually' past the Schwarzschild radius. The paper appears on 1 September 1939 — the day Germany invades Poland. It is ignored for decades.
moments.takeaway: Black holes are predicted as inevitable. The world looks elsewhere.

moments.title: Wheeler coins 'black hole'
moments.body: Wheeler popularises the term 'black hole' at a 1967 conference. The French initially object as it sounds obscene in translation. Wheeler famously summarises GR as: 'Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.'
moments.takeaway: A good name makes a phenomenon thinkable.

moments.title: Cygnus X-1
moments.body: X-ray emission from Cygnus X-1 plus orbital dynamics indicate a compact object of ~14 solar masses orbiting a blue supergiant — the first widely accepted stellar black hole. Hawking and Thorne bet on it (Hawking betting it isn't a black hole, as a 'consolation' if his life's work proved wrong). Hawking pays up in 1990.
moments.takeaway: Astronomical observation confirms the existence of black holes.

moments.title: First image of a black hole
moments.body: The EHT releases the first image of M87*'s shadow. The bright ring matches GR predictions to 10%. In 2022 they image Sagittarius A* at the centre of our galaxy.
moments.takeaway: A century after Schwarzschild, we can photograph what he predicted.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Sagittarius A* is 4.3 million solar masses. The largest known is TON 618 at ~66 billion solar masses. Hawking's prediction that black holes evaporate via quantum emission remains experimentally unverified.
now.open_questions: What's inside the event horizon? Where does the information go? Is the singularity real?

items.reflection: Einstein himself did not believe black holes were physical. Even theorists distrust their own theories' wilder consequences. Why?

moments.title: Baade and Zwicky predict neutron stars
moments.body: Zwicky and Baade propose that supernovae are powered by the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star — an object so dense it is essentially a giant atomic nucleus. The paper is mostly ignored. Zwicky also predicts dark matter and gravitational lensing; he is decades ahead.
moments.takeaway: Neutron stars predicted within two years of the neutron's discovery.

moments.title: Bell Burnell's 'little green men'
moments.body: PhD student Jocelyn Bell, analysing miles of chart paper from a new radio telescope, finds a faint pulsing signal with 1.337-second period. She and her supervisor jokingly label it LGM-1 (Little Green Men). More pulsars follow. They are spinning neutron stars. Hewish wins the 1974 Nobel; Bell Burnell is omitted.
moments.takeaway: A graduate student spots cosmic lighthouses and is excluded from the prize.

moments.title: Hulse-Taylor binary
moments.body: A binary pulsar is discovered. Over years, its orbital period decays at exactly the rate predicted by general relativity for gravitational wave emission. This is the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves. Hulse and Taylor win the 1993 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Pulsar timing confirms gravitational waves four decades before LIGO.

moments.title: Multi-messenger astronomy
moments.body: GW170817 — gravitational waves from a neutron-star merger — is detected, followed seconds later by a gamma-ray burst and over the following weeks by light at every wavelength. The event creates ~10 Earth masses of gold and platinum.
moments.takeaway: Multi-messenger astronomy is born. The origin of gold is solved.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Roughly 3,000 pulsars are known. Millisecond pulsars are used as cosmic clocks. The densest neutron stars are about twice the Sun's mass packed into 20 km.
now.open_questions: What is the equation of state of dense nuclear matter? Are quark stars real?

items.reflection: Bell Burnell received many awards later, including the £2.3M Special Breakthrough Prize (donated to physics scholarships for under-represented groups). What does her response say about scientific recognition?

moments.title: Hooke's spring law
moments.body: Hooke discovers the linear relation between force and extension for springs. He encodes it as a Latin anagram (CEIIINOSSSTTUV) to claim priority while keeping the result secret. Decoded: 'Ut tensio, sic vis' — as the extension, so the force.

quote.text: Ut tensio, sic vis.

moments.takeaway: Materials science begins with a hidden Latin pun.

moments.title: Young's modulus
moments.body: Young generalises Hooke's law to materials, defining E = stress/strain. The 'modulus of elasticity' becomes the central concept in solid mechanics. Young also did the double-slit experiment, theory of capillarity, and partial decipherment of the Rosetta Stone.
moments.takeaway: Young's modulus links Hooke's spring to all elastic solids.

moments.title: Cauchy's stress tensor
moments.body: Cauchy develops the tensor theory of stress, treating each direction in a material separately. The Cauchy stress tensor underpins all modern continuum mechanics.
moments.takeaway: Stress becomes a tensor, not a number.

moments.title: X-ray crystallography
moments.who: William Henry Bragg, William Lawrence Bragg
moments.body: Father and son derive the Bragg condition (2d sin theta = n lambda) for X-ray diffraction by crystals. They share the 1915 Nobel; Lawrence at 25 is still the youngest physics laureate. The technique will eventually reveal DNA, proteins, drugs and materials.
moments.takeaway: Materials science can now see atomic arrangements.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Materials science now spans aluminium aircraft, carbon-fibre composites, semiconductors, graphene, metamaterials, and self-healing polymers. Finite-element analysis lets engineers simulate stresses before manufacture.
now.open_questions: Can we design materials atom-by-atom for arbitrary properties?

items.reflection: Hooke wrote his law as an anagram to keep it secret. Modern open science discourages this. What changed in scientific culture?

moments.title: Braun rectifies a crystal
moments.body: Braun discovers that some crystal contacts allow current to flow one way more easily than the other — the first semiconductor rectifier. He shares the 1909 Nobel with Marconi. The physics is mysterious.
moments.takeaway: Semiconductor physics begins with a phenomenon no one understands.

moments.title: Bell Labs transistor
moments.who: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, William Shockley
moments.body: On 23 December 1947, Bardeen and Brattain demonstrate the point-contact transistor. Shockley, frustrated to be left off, develops the superior junction transistor weeks later. They share the 1956 Nobel. Their relationships collapse acrimoniously. Bardeen later wins a second Nobel for superconductivity (BCS theory, 1972).
moments.takeaway: The transistor is invented — and the inventors fall out.

moments.title: Integrated circuit
moments.body: Kilby builds the first IC out of germanium; Noyce builds one out of silicon with planar interconnects. Kilby wins the 2000 Nobel; Noyce, who died in 1990, cannot share it. Noyce co-founds Intel.
moments.takeaway: Multiple transistors on one chip — the foundation of all modern electronics.

moments.title: Moore's law
moments.body: Moore predicts the number of transistors per chip will double every two years. The 'law' holds, with adjustments, for 60 years. From dozens of transistors in 1965 to over 100 billion per modern chip.
moments.takeaway: An empirical observation drives the most consequential industrial roadmap in history.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern chips contain ~100 billion transistors with feature sizes of a few nanometres. TSMC's 3 nm process is at the physical limits. The global semiconductor industry is worth ~$600 billion annually.
now.open_questions: What replaces silicon? Quantum, neuromorphic, carbon nanotubes?

items.reflection: The transistor's three inventors despised each other. Shockley became a notorious eugenicist. How should we honour discoverers whose later lives reflect badly on them?

moments.title: Heisenberg on Helgoland
moments.body: Suffering from hay fever, 23-year-old Heisenberg retreats to the rocky island of Helgoland. In a fever of insight, he abandons electron orbits in favour of arrays of observable quantities multiplied non-commutatively. He returns to Göttingen with matrix mechanics — the first complete quantum theory.

quote.text: It was almost three o'clock in the morning before the final result of my computations lay before me... I was deeply alarmed.

moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics is born in a single night on a desolate island.

moments.title: The uncertainty paper
moments.body: Heisenberg derives Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2. You cannot simultaneously know a particle's position and momentum with arbitrary precision — not because of measurement limits but because of the structure of the theory.
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics imposes fundamental limits on knowledge.

moments.title: EPR and entanglement
moments.body: Einstein and colleagues argue quantum mechanics must be incomplete, because pairs of particles can be correlated across arbitrary distance ('spooky action at a distance'). Schrödinger, replying, coins the word 'entanglement'.
moments.takeaway: Einstein attacks quantum mechanics; in doing so he invents the concept of entanglement, central decades later.

moments.title: Bell's theorem
moments.body: Bell proves that no local hidden variable theory can reproduce all quantum predictions. Bell tests by Clauser/Freedman (1972), Aspect (1982), and loophole-free experiments in 2015 decisively rule out local realism.
moments.takeaway: Einstein was wrong. Quantum entanglement is real and violates local realism.

moments.title: Nobel for Bell tests
moments.body: The 2022 Nobel goes to three pioneers of Bell-inequality experiments. Their work now underpins quantum cryptography and quantum computing.
moments.takeaway: An apparently philosophical question — is reality local? — becomes industrial.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Quantum information science is now a major technology field. Quantum key distribution is commercial. Quantum computers (IBM, Google, IonQ) operate with hundreds of qubits. Entanglement has been demonstrated across 1,200+ km (Micius satellite).
now.open_questions: What collapses the wave function? Is entanglement the basic stuff of spacetime?

items.reflection: Heisenberg later worked on the Nazi nuclear programme; Bohr fled to America. How does totalitarianism distort science?

moments.title: Schrödinger in the Alps
moments.body: Schrödinger, 38, takes Christmas holiday in the Alps with an unidentified woman (not his wife). Inspired by de Broglie's matter waves, he derives a wave equation for the electron. In weeks he solves hydrogen, harmonic oscillator, and rotor.
moments.takeaway: The most important equation in chemistry is derived during a mountain affair.

moments.title: Born's probability interpretation
moments.body: Born proposes that |psi|^2 gives the probability density of finding a particle. The wave function is not a real wave but a probability amplitude. Einstein objects: 'God does not play dice.' Born wins the 1954 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The wave function is a probability — not a physical wave.

moments.title: Dirac unifies quantum and relativity
moments.body: Dirac, 25, writes a relativistic wave equation for the electron. The solutions include both electrons and a mysterious 'antiparticle' with the same mass but opposite charge. Four years later Anderson finds the positron in cloud-chamber photographs.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics predicts antimatter before anyone observes it.

moments.title: Schrödinger's cat
moments.body: Schrödinger devises a thought experiment in which a cat is sealed in a box with a radioactive trigger. Until observation, the cat is in a superposition of alive and dead. He intends this as a reductio ad absurdum of the Copenhagen interpretation. It becomes the most famous illustration of quantum weirdness.

quote.text: I don't like it, and I'm sorry I ever had anything to do with it.

moments.takeaway: The inventor of the wave equation comes to dislike his own creation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Schrödinger equation underlies all of quantum chemistry. Density functional theory computes molecular structures for millions of molecules. Quantum chemistry is central to drug discovery and materials design.
now.open_questions: Is wave function collapse a real physical process?

items.reflection: Schrödinger built the equation; he disliked the interpretation. Why are some scientists alienated by the consequences of their own work?

moments.title: Fourier's heat equation
moments.body: Napoleon's former Egyptian campaign administrator, now Prefect of Isère, presents 'Théorie analytique de la chaleur' to the Paris Academy. He claims any periodic function can be expanded as a sum of sines and cosines. Lagrange and Laplace are unconvinced. The work is rejected in 1807 and finally published in 1822.
moments.takeaway: Fourier's theorem — initially rejected by the greatest mathematicians — becomes a cornerstone of mathematical physics.

moments.title: Helmholtz and the ear
moments.body: Helmholtz applies Fourier analysis to acoustics in 'On the Sensations of Tone'. He shows the cochlea decomposes sound into frequencies — the ear performs a Fourier transform.
moments.takeaway: The ear is a biological Fourier analyser.

moments.title: Fast Fourier Transform
moments.body: Cooley and Tukey publish the FFT algorithm, reducing Fourier computation from N^2 to N log N operations. The algorithm, it turns out, was known to Gauss in 1805 and forgotten. The FFT is now one of the ten most important algorithms of the 20th century.
moments.takeaway: Gauss invented it; Cooley and Tukey rediscovered it; the world now runs on it.

moments.title: Fourier everywhere
moments.body: Fourier transforms appear in MRI scanners, JPEG compression, MP3 audio, speech recognition, seismology, radio astronomy, quantum mechanics, and signal processing of every kind. Every smartphone runs millions of FFTs per second.
moments.takeaway: A heat equation from 1807 powers modern signal processing.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Fourier methods are universal in physics and engineering. Wavelet analysis extends them to time-frequency localisation. Quantum Fourier transform is central to Shor's algorithm and quantum computing.
now.open_questions: Can quantum Fourier methods deliver practical advantage on noisy quantum computers?

items.reflection: Fourier's theorem was rejected by Lagrange and Laplace — the leading mathematicians of the day. When should you trust intuition over authority?

moments.title: Einstein predicts GWs
moments.body: Einstein derives gravitational waves from his field equations — ripples in spacetime travelling at the speed of light. He later doubts his own prediction and in 1936 submits a paper claiming GWs don't exist; a referee corrects him.
moments.takeaway: Even Einstein doubted Einstein.

moments.title: Pirani and Weber
moments.body: Pirani shows GWs would have a physical effect on test masses. Weber builds the first 'bar detector' — a 2-ton aluminium cylinder. In 1969 he claims detection; nobody can reproduce his results.
moments.takeaway: The first false alarm in GW astronomy.

moments.title: Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar
moments.body: PSR B1913+16, a binary pulsar, loses orbital energy at exactly the rate GR predicts for GW emission. The 1993 Nobel goes to Hulse and Taylor for the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves.
moments.takeaway: Indirect detection precedes direct by 41 years.

moments.title: GW150914
moments.body: On 14 September 2015, both LIGO detectors register a chirping signal — the merger of two ~30 solar-mass black holes, 1.3 billion light years away. The signal lasts 0.2 seconds and matches GR templates perfectly. The 2017 Nobel goes to Weiss, Barish and Thorne.
moments.takeaway: A century after Einstein's prediction, spacetime ripples are heard.

moments.title: GW170817 — neutron star merger
moments.body: GWs and a gamma-ray burst arrive within 2 seconds of each other from a neutron-star merger. Optical telescopes worldwide observe the 'kilonova' that creates ~10 Earth masses of gold and platinum.
moments.takeaway: The gold in your wedding ring comes from neutron-star collisions.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: LIGO and Virgo have detected ~100 merger events since 2015. LISA, a space-based detector launching ~2035, will detect supermassive black-hole mergers. Pulsar timing arrays (NANOGrav, 2023) detect the stochastic GW background.
now.open_questions: What is the maximum mass of a neutron star? Are primordial black holes real?

items.reflection: Einstein doubted his own prediction. The detection required strain sensitivity of 10^-21 — a hundred-million-millionth of an atom. How do we build instruments to measure what we can barely believe in?

moments.title: Dirac's equation
moments.body: Dirac, 25, writes a relativistic wave equation for the electron. The solutions include negative-energy states. Dirac proposes these are a 'sea' of filled electrons; 'holes' in this sea behave as positive particles.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics predicts a previously unknown form of matter.

moments.title: Anderson photographs the positron
moments.body: Anderson, examining cosmic-ray cloud-chamber photographs, finds tracks curving the wrong way — a positively charged particle with the mass of an electron. He calls it the positron. He wins the 1936 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Antimatter exists. Dirac's prediction is confirmed in cosmic rays.

moments.title: Antiproton
moments.body: The Berkeley Bevatron produces antiprotons by smashing protons together. Antimatter is no longer a cosmic-ray curiosity — it can be made in the lab.
moments.takeaway: Antimatter becomes a laboratory reality.

moments.title: Antihydrogen at CERN
moments.body: CERN's antiproton decelerator produces and traps antihydrogen atoms. In 2023 ALPHA shows antihydrogen falls down in gravity, not up — antimatter feels gravity normally.
moments.takeaway: Antimatter atoms can be made, trapped and probed. They behave like matter atoms.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Antimatter is used in PET scanners (positron emission tomography) for cancer imaging. CERN holds tens of antihydrogen atoms in magnetic traps. The cost of making 1 gram of antimatter: ~$60 trillion.
now.open_questions: Why is the universe overwhelmingly matter, not antimatter? What broke the symmetry?

items.reflection: Dirac predicted antimatter from pure algebra. He once said 'a theory with mathematical beauty is more likely to be correct than one which is ugly'. Is beauty a reliable guide?

moments.title: Onnes' mercury
moments.body: Onnes liquefies helium in 1908 — the last gas to be liquefied. In 1911 he cools mercury below 4.2 K and finds its resistance suddenly drops to zero. He wins the 1913 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Mercury becomes a perfect conductor below 4.2 K. No one knows why.

moments.title: Meissner effect
moments.body: They discover that superconductors expel magnetic fields entirely — not just because of perfect conductivity, but as an intrinsic property. The Meissner effect is the smoking-gun signature of superconductivity.
moments.takeaway: Superconductors levitate magnets. The effect is thermodynamic, not just electrical.

moments.title: BCS theory
moments.who: John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, Robert Schrieffer
moments.body: Bardeen (already a Nobel laureate for the transistor), Cooper and Schrieffer explain superconductivity. Electrons form 'Cooper pairs' via phonon (lattice vibration) exchange and condense into a single quantum state. Bardeen becomes the only person to win two physics Nobels (1972).
moments.takeaway: After 46 years, superconductivity is finally understood.

moments.title: High-T_c cuprates
moments.body: They discover superconductivity in a copper-oxide ceramic at 35 K — far above the limit predicted by BCS theory. The 1987 Nobel comes quickly. Soon, YBCO is found to superconduct above 77 K (liquid nitrogen).
moments.takeaway: Ceramics — usually insulators — superconduct at temperatures no one thought possible.

moments.title: Room-temperature SC (controversy)
moments.body: A 2020 Nature paper claims superconductivity at 15°C under 270 GPa pressure (a million atmospheres). The result is retracted in 2022. A 2023 'LK-99' claim collapses within weeks. The hunt continues.
moments.takeaway: Room-temperature superconductivity remains the holy grail — and a source of high-profile retractions.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Superconducting magnets power MRI scanners and the LHC. Quantum computers use superconducting qubits. The highest confirmed T_c is ~250 K in hydrogen sulphide at 150 GPa. No one yet understands cuprate superconductivity.
now.open_questions: Is room-pressure room-temperature superconductivity possible? What is the mechanism in cuprates?

items.reflection: BCS theory took 46 years; cuprate theory is still missing 38 years later. Why is some physics so resistant to theoretical understanding?

moments.title: Maxwell's demon and gas kinetics
moments.body: Maxwell derives the distribution of molecular speeds in a gas — the first statistical law in physics. He later devises 'Maxwell's demon': a being who could sort fast from slow molecules and apparently violate the second law.
moments.takeaway: The first statistical law in physics.

moments.title: Boltzmann's S = k log W
moments.body: Boltzmann shows entropy is statistical: S = k log W, where W counts the number of microstates corresponding to a macrostate. The second law is overwhelming probability, not absolute necessity.
moments.takeaway: Entropy is counting. The deepest law in classical physics is a statement about probability.

moments.title: Atomism wars
moments.body: Mach and Ostwald — 'energeticists' — deny atoms exist. They harass Boltzmann publicly. His depression deepens.
moments.takeaway: At the height of his career, Boltzmann is attacked for believing in atoms.

moments.title: Boltzmann's suicide
moments.body: On holiday on the Adriatic, Boltzmann hangs himself. He dies just years before Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion conclusively confirms the existence of atoms. S = k log W is later carved on his tombstone in Vienna.
moments.takeaway: Boltzmann dies before atoms are confirmed. Vindication comes too late.

moments.title: Shannon entropy
moments.body: Shannon defines information entropy with exactly Boltzmann's mathematical form. Von Neumann tells him to call it 'entropy' because 'nobody knows what entropy really is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage'.
moments.takeaway: Entropy unites thermodynamics, information theory, biology and cosmology.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Statistical mechanics underpins materials science, chemistry, biology, computer science and cosmology. Maxwell's demon survives — Landauer's principle (1961) shows information erasure has a thermodynamic cost.
now.open_questions: Why is the universe's initial entropy so low? What is the arrow of time?

items.reflection: Boltzmann was attacked by physicists who refused to accept atoms. He died before atoms were confirmed. How should we treat ideas that look right but can't yet be tested?

moments.title: Lee and Yang ask the question
moments.who: T. D. Lee, C. N. Yang, Brookhaven
moments.body: Two young Chinese-American theorists puzzle over the 'theta-tau puzzle': two particles that look identical except one decays into two pions, the other into three. The two modes have opposite parity. They propose: maybe parity isn't conserved in weak interactions.
moments.takeaway: A puzzle about kaon decays suggests left and right are not equivalent at fundamental level.

moments.title: Wu's cobalt experiment
moments.body:
Wu, a Columbia experimentalist, cools cobalt-60 to near absolute zero and aligns nuclei in a magnetic field. Beta decay produces more electrons in one direction than the other. Parity is violated.

Lee and Yang win the 1957 Nobel within months. Wu is omitted.
moments.takeaway: Nature does distinguish left from right. Yet another woman is left off the Nobel.

moments.title: CP violation
moments.body: Cronin and Fitch find that even CP (charge + parity) is violated in kaon decays — at the part-per-thousand level. They win the 1980 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Even with charge conjugation, left and right are not perfectly mirror-symmetric.

moments.title: BaBar, Belle, LHCb
moments.body: Modern experiments measure CP violation in B-mesons. The observed CP violation is too small to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe; new physics must exist somewhere.
moments.takeaway: The asymmetry of matter over antimatter remains unexplained.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Parity violation is built into the standard model via the V-A weak interaction. CP violation is measured in many systems. CPT (charge + parity + time) symmetry remains universally conserved.
now.open_questions: Why is the universe matter-dominated? Is the CKM matrix the whole story?

items.reflection: Wu's experiment is one of the most-cited Nobel omissions in physics. How should communities correct historic injustice?

moments.title: Röntgen's mysterious rays
moments.body:
Working with a Crookes tube in a darkened room, Röntgen sees a fluorescent screen glow across the room. The radiation passes through cardboard, books, even flesh — revealing the bones of his wife's hand on a photographic plate. He calls them 'X' rays for unknown.

He wins the 1901 Nobel — the very first physics Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A new kind of radiation, the first medical imaging, the first physics Nobel — all from one accidental observation.

moments.title: Laue's diffraction
moments.body: Laue suspects X-rays are short electromagnetic waves and crystals are regular atomic arrays. He fires X-rays through a copper sulphate crystal and sees a diffraction pattern. Two predictions confirmed at once.
moments.takeaway: X-rays are waves and crystals are lattices.

moments.title: Bragg's law
moments.body: Father and son derive 2d sin theta = n lambda. Lawrence, at 25, is the youngest physics Nobel laureate ever (1915). The Braggs determine the structures of salt, diamond, and many other crystals.
moments.takeaway: Crystal structures can now be determined atom by atom.

moments.title: DNA double helix
moments.body: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction Photo 51 — shown to Watson without her permission — reveals the DNA double helix. Crick and Watson model it; Wilkins shares the 1962 Nobel. Franklin had died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at 37.
moments.takeaway: X-ray crystallography unlocks the molecule of life.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) image single biomolecules. Synchrotrons routinely solve protein structures for drug discovery. Crystallography has won at least 28 Nobel Prizes across physics, chemistry and medicine.
now.open_questions: Can XFELs image proteins at room temperature in real time?

items.reflection: Röntgen refused to patent his discovery, saying it should benefit humanity. How should fundamental discoveries be owned, if at all?

moments.title: Bose's photon statistics
moments.body: A young Indian lecturer derives Planck's blackbody law by treating photons as indistinguishable particles obeying a new statistics. He sends the paper to Einstein, who translates it into German and gets it published. Einstein extends it to massive particles.
moments.takeaway: A colonial physicist invents one of two fundamental statistics in nature.

moments.title: Fermi-Dirac statistics
moments.body: Fermi and Dirac independently derive the other quantum statistics: particles that cannot occupy the same state. The Pauli exclusion principle. Fermions vs bosons becomes the basic dichotomy of matter.
moments.takeaway: All particles in the universe are either fermions or bosons.

moments.title: First Bose-Einstein condensate
moments.body: Cornell and Wieman cool rubidium atoms to 170 nanokelvin in JILA, Boulder. The atoms collapse into a single quantum state — the long-predicted Bose-Einstein condensate. Ketterle at MIT does the same with sodium months later. They share the 2001 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A new state of matter, predicted 70 years earlier, is finally made in the lab.

moments.title: Quantum simulation
moments.body: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices simulate condensed-matter Hamiltonians. They are used to test models of high-T_c superconductivity, the Hubbard model, and topological phases.
moments.takeaway: Atoms become analog computers for solid-state physics.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: BECs are routine in dozens of labs worldwide. Atomic interferometers use cold atoms to measure gravity, rotations and the fine-structure constant. Quantum gas microscopes image individual atoms in lattices.
now.open_questions: Can analog quantum simulators solve problems classical computers cannot?

items.reflection: Bose's paper was rejected by a journal before Einstein recognised it. How should we identify good science from outside the mainstream?

moments.title: Tycho's island observatory
moments.body: Funded by the Danish king with an entire island, Tycho builds the largest, most precise observatory in the world — accurate to 1/60 of a degree, all done by naked eye. He observes the heavens for 25 years before quarrelling with the new king and moving to Prague.
moments.takeaway: A nobleman, a metal nose (lost in a duel) and the most precise pre-telescopic observations ever made.

moments.title: Kepler joins Tycho
moments.body: Kepler — a Lutheran refugee, mathematician, mystic — becomes Tycho's assistant. Tycho dies the next year, allegedly of a bladder rupture from politeness at a long dinner. Kepler inherits the data.
moments.takeaway: The richest astronomical dataset of the era passes to a poor mystic mathematician.

moments.title: Three laws
moments.body: Kepler spends 8 years on Mars alone. The orbit is an ellipse, not a circle. He formulates three laws: orbits are ellipses; equal areas in equal times; T^2 proportional to a^3. He believes the cosmos is musical and Platonic; he discovers physics anyway.
moments.takeaway: Empirical laws of planetary motion, derived from one obsessive analysis of Mars.

moments.title: Newton derives Kepler
moments.body: Newton shows Kepler's three empirical laws follow from a single inverse-square gravitational force. The two-body problem is solved exactly.
moments.takeaway: Kepler's three laws are unified into one — Newton's gravity.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Kepler's laws underpin all orbital mechanics — satellites, interplanetary probes, exoplanet detection. NASA's Kepler space telescope (named after him) found 2,600 exoplanets by transit photometry.
now.open_questions: How accurately can we determine masses of multi-planet systems from Kepler-style timing?

items.reflection: Kepler believed the cosmos was musical and Platonic. His mysticism led him to seek patterns — and find real laws. When does pseudoscience accidentally produce science?

moments.title: Cherenkov sees the glow
moments.body: Cherenkov, a Soviet graduate student, notices a faint blue glow when radium emits radiation into water. The glow comes from charged particles travelling faster than light in the medium (though not faster than light in vacuum).
moments.takeaway: Particles can travel faster than light — in water.

moments.title: Frank and Tamm explain
moments.body: Frank and Tamm derive the theory: when a charged particle exceeds c/n in a medium, it emits an electromagnetic shockwave — the optical analogue of a sonic boom.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov radiation is the light equivalent of a sonic boom.

moments.title: Nobel Prize
moments.body: The three share the 1958 Nobel. Cherenkov detectors become standard in particle physics for identifying high-speed particles by their characteristic ring of light.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov detection is now a workhorse of particle physics.

moments.title: Super-Kamiokande and IceCube
moments.body: Super-Kamiokande (50,000 tonnes of water) and IceCube (a cubic km of Antarctic ice) detect Cherenkov light from neutrino interactions. SN 1987A neutrinos and TeV cosmic neutrinos are caught this way.
moments.takeaway: Cherenkov rings reveal the neutrino sky.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cherenkov radiation is used in IACT (Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes), particle accelerators, nuclear reactors (the iconic blue glow), and astroparticle physics. CTA, a next-generation Cherenkov array, is under construction in Spain and Chile.
now.open_questions: What are the sources of PeV cosmic neutrinos?

items.reflection: Cherenkov nearly didn't believe his own observation. He repeated it for years before publication. When should you doubt a clear experimental result?

moments.title: Bekenstein's entropy
moments.body: Bekenstein, a graduate student, argues black holes must have entropy proportional to their horizon area. Hawking and his collaborators initially dismiss the claim.
moments.takeaway: A graduate student attaches thermodynamics to general relativity. The senior physicists object.

moments.title: Hawking radiation
moments.body: Hawking applies quantum field theory near a black hole horizon. To his astonishment, black holes are not black — they emit thermal radiation. T ~ 1/M. They evaporate. Bekenstein was right.
moments.takeaway: Black holes are quantum mechanical. They have temperature, entropy, and a finite lifetime.

moments.title: Information paradox
moments.body: Hawking argues that black-hole evaporation destroys information — violating quantum mechanics. Decades of debate follow. Hawking bets against information preservation; he loses the bet in 2004.
moments.takeaway: The black-hole information paradox is the deepest puzzle in quantum gravity.

moments.title: Page curves and islands
moments.body: Calculations using the AdS/CFT correspondence and quantum extremal surfaces give a Page curve for evaporating black holes consistent with information preservation. The 'island' formula is celebrated; the mechanism is still debated.
moments.takeaway: Information is probably preserved. How is unclear.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Hawking radiation has never been directly observed; for a solar-mass black hole, T = 60 nK. Analogue Hawking radiation has been seen in sonic black holes (Steinhauer, 2016).
now.open_questions: What is inside a black hole? How is information preserved?

items.reflection: Hawking changed his mind publicly about information preservation. How should scientists handle being wrong on their most famous claim?

moments.title: Maxwell's demon
moments.body: Maxwell imagines a being who could sort fast molecules from slow without doing work, decreasing entropy and violating the second law. He calls it a 'finite being'; Lord Kelvin later names it the 'demon'.
moments.takeaway: A thought experiment that seems to violate the second law.

moments.title: Szilárd's engine
moments.body: Szilárd reformulates the demon. A one-molecule heat engine can extract kT ln 2 of work per bit of information. He shows the demon's measurement, not its sorting, must produce entropy.
moments.takeaway: Information is physical. Each bit has thermodynamic value.

moments.title: Landauer's principle
moments.body: Landauer shows that erasing one bit of information requires at least kT ln 2 of energy as heat. Computation can in principle be reversible and free; only erasure costs.
moments.takeaway: Information erasure is the only thermodynamically costly step in computing.

moments.title: Landauer confirmed experimentally
moments.body: The Landauer bound is confirmed in a single-particle experiment. Erasing one bit really does cost kT ln 2.
moments.takeaway: Landauer is right. Information is thermodynamic.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern processors dissipate 10^9 times more than the Landauer bound per logical operation. Reversible and quantum computing aim to approach the bound.
now.open_questions: Can computation be made physically reversible at scale?

items.reflection: A 19th-century thought experiment turns out to govern 21st-century computing limits. How often does deep theoretical physics predict practical engineering bounds?

moments.title: Joule's brewery
moments.body: A wealthy brewer's son, Joule does experiments at his parents' brewery and home laboratory. He measures the mechanical equivalent of heat using a paddle wheel stirring water. 4.18 joules of mechanical work raises the water temperature exactly as 1 calorie of heat would.
moments.takeaway: Heat and mechanical work are forms of the same thing: energy.

moments.title: Mayer's independent derivation
moments.body: A German ship's surgeon notices that venous blood is redder in the tropics than in Europe — bodies need less heat in warm climates. He derives the mechanical equivalent of heat from gas physics. He is ignored, ridiculed, attempts suicide.
moments.takeaway: Independent discovery, rejection, breakdown. Vindication comes late.

moments.title: Helmholtz formalises
moments.body: Helmholtz publishes 'Über die Erhaltung der Kraft' — On the Conservation of Force [Energy]. He shows energy conservation must apply universally if perpetual motion is impossible.
moments.takeaway: Energy conservation becomes a fundamental law of physics.

moments.title: Noether's theorem
moments.body: Noether shows energy conservation is a consequence of time-translation symmetry. The first law of thermodynamics has its deepest explanation.
moments.takeaway: Energy is conserved because the laws of physics don't change in time.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Energy conservation is among the most reliable laws in physics. In general relativity, however, global energy conservation is subtle — energy of cosmological scales is ill-defined.
now.open_questions: Is dark energy 'energy' in the strict sense? Where does it come from?

items.reflection: Mayer was ignored; Joule was rich; Helmholtz had institutional power. How does class shape who is heard in science?

moments.title: Brown's pollen
moments.body: Botanist Robert Brown, observing pollen suspended in water, notices the grains jiggle erratically. He checks that non-living particles do the same; the motion is not biological. He cannot explain it.
moments.takeaway: A botanist sees molecular motion without realising what it is.

moments.title: Einstein's Brownian paper
moments.body: Einstein, in one of his miracle-year papers, shows Brownian motion is the result of bombardment by water molecules. He derives a formula linking the random-walk displacement to Avogadro's number and the Boltzmann constant.
moments.takeaway: Einstein turns Brown's jiggle into a measurement of Avogadro's number.

moments.title: Perrin measures Avogadro
moments.body: Perrin painstakingly measures Brownian motion of gamboge particles. He gets Avogadro's number to within 10% of the modern value. The energeticists' opposition collapses; even Ostwald concedes atoms exist. Perrin wins the 1926 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Atoms are experimentally confirmed via the dance of pollen.

moments.title: Wiener formalises
moments.body: Wiener defines Brownian motion mathematically as a stochastic process. The Wiener process underlies modern finance (Black-Scholes), control theory and stochastic differential equations.
moments.takeaway: Brownian motion becomes the canonical stochastic process in mathematics.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Brownian motion underlies diffusion in cells, transport in batteries, polymer dynamics, and quantitative finance. Single-molecule biology routinely tracks individual proteins via Brownian motion.
now.open_questions: Can biological motors fully escape Brownian noise? How efficient is ATP synthase?

items.reflection: Brown saw the motion in 1827. Einstein explained it in 1905. Why did it take 78 years for the right explanation to arrive?

moments.title: Poincaré and the three-body problem
moments.body: Competing for King Oscar II's prize on the stability of the solar system, Poincaré discovers the three-body problem has chaotic solutions: tiny changes in initial conditions produce vastly different futures. He wins the prize despite a mistake in his original submission.
moments.takeaway: Determinism does not imply predictability. The seed of chaos theory is planted in 1889.

moments.title: Lorenz and the weather
moments.body: Running a weather simulation, Lorenz restarts a computation with a printed number — 0.506 instead of the stored 0.506127. The forecast diverges completely. He coins the 'butterfly effect': a butterfly flapping in Brazil might set off a tornado in Texas.
moments.takeaway: Weather is intrinsically unpredictable past a horizon of about two weeks.

moments.title: 'Chaos' named
moments.body: Yorke and Li publish 'Period Three Implies Chaos', giving the field its name. Mandelbrot's fractals (1975 book) become its visual signature.
moments.takeaway: A new field of physics — chaos theory — emerges from a paper on iteration.

moments.title: Chaos everywhere
moments.body: Chaos is found in heartbeats, lasers, ecology, fluid flow, chemical reactions, and the solar system itself. Yet chaotic systems can have statistical predictability: the climate is not the weather.
moments.takeaway: Determinism + sensitivity to initial conditions = practical unpredictability.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Numerical weather prediction extends to ~14 days. Climate models project century-scale statistics. Chaos in the solar system means planetary orbits are unpredictable past ~50 million years.
now.open_questions: How do we forecast extreme weather despite chaos? Can we ever predict turbulence?
