items.reflection: Lorenz's discovery came from sloppy data entry. How often do accidents reveal physics?

moments.title: Einstein's cosmological constant
moments.body: Applying GR to the universe, Einstein finds it must be expanding or contracting. He adds a term Lambda to keep it static. After Hubble shows expansion, he calls Lambda his 'biggest blunder'.
moments.takeaway: Einstein invents dark energy in 1917 and rejects it in 1929. He was right the first time.

moments.title: Two supernova teams
moments.who: Saul Perlmutter (LBL); Brian Schmidt, Adam Riess (Harvard/Mt Stromlo)
moments.body: Two competing teams use Type Ia supernovae — 'standardisable candles' — to measure the universe's expansion at large distances. The aim is to measure the deceleration of expansion due to gravity.
moments.takeaway: Two rival teams race to measure cosmic deceleration.

moments.title: Acceleration discovered
moments.body: Both teams find the universe's expansion is accelerating, not decelerating. Distant supernovae are dimmer than expected. Something — 'dark energy' — is pushing the universe apart. Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess share the 2011 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: 68% of the universe is mysterious. Einstein's 'blunder' returns.

moments.title: DESI hints at evolving dark energy
moments.body: DESI's results show possible evolution of the dark-energy equation of state — at 2-4 sigma. If confirmed, the simple cosmological constant model is wrong.
moments.takeaway: Dark energy may not be a constant after all.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Dark energy makes up 68% of the universe. Its nature is unknown. Euclid (launched 2023), Roman Space Telescope (2027) and Vera Rubin Observatory will refine measurements.
now.open_questions: Is dark energy the cosmological constant or something dynamic? Why is its value so small?

items.reflection: Einstein called Lambda his biggest blunder. The 2011 Nobel essentially restored it. Can you be wrong about being wrong?

moments.title: Fraunhofer's dark lines
moments.body: A self-taught optician finds hundreds of dark lines in the solar spectrum. He maps and catalogues them, naming the main ones A through K. He dies young; the lines remain a mystery for decades.
moments.takeaway: The Sun's spectrum has hundreds of unexplained dark lines.

moments.title: Bunsen and Kirchhoff
moments.body: Using Bunsen's clean-flame burner and a prism, they show every element gives a characteristic emission spectrum. They explain Fraunhofer lines as absorption of solar light by elements in the Sun's atmosphere. They discover caesium and rubidium.
moments.takeaway: Spectroscopy is born. Stars can be chemically analysed without going to them.

moments.title: Helium found in the Sun
moments.body: During a solar eclipse, Janssen sees a yellow line. Lockyer attributes it to a new element — helium, from helios (sun). It is not found on Earth until 1895 (Ramsay).
moments.takeaway: An element is discovered on the Sun 27 years before being found on Earth.

moments.title: Balmer's formula
moments.body: A schoolteacher derives an empirical formula for the visible hydrogen lines. Rydberg generalises it. The formula is exact but unexplained — until Bohr in 1913.
moments.takeaway: A schoolteacher's formula encodes quantum mechanics 28 years early.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Spectroscopy is one of the most powerful tools in science. It measures chemical compositions of exoplanet atmospheres (JWST), galaxy redshifts (DESI), and individual atoms in dilution refrigerators.
now.open_questions: Can spectroscopy of exoplanet atmospheres detect biosignatures?

items.reflection: Balmer's empirical formula was correct decades before any theoretical explanation. How important are unexplained empirical patterns in physics?

moments.title: Dirac predicts monopoles
moments.body: Dirac shows that if even one magnetic monopole exists anywhere in the universe, all electric charge must be quantised. He calls the conclusion 'one of the strangest in physics'.
moments.takeaway: Charge quantisation might be a consequence of monopoles.

moments.title: GUT monopoles
moments.body: Grand Unified Theories predict heavy magnetic monopoles (~10^16 GeV). If inflation occurred, almost all would have been diluted away.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical monopoles enter cosmology.

moments.title: Cabrera's Valentine's Day event
moments.body: On 14 February 1982, Cabrera's superconducting loop registers a single event consistent with a monopole passing through. The event is never reproduced. Was it real?
moments.takeaway: One of the most tantalising single events in physics history.

moments.title: Still nothing
moments.body: Searches with MoEDAL (LHC), IceCube and direct-detection experiments have found no monopoles. Limits exclude vast regions of parameter space.
moments.takeaway: If monopoles exist, they are extraordinarily rare.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Monopoles are predicted by most GUTs. None has been observed. Analogue monopoles (Dirac strings) have been simulated in spin ice and BECs.
now.open_questions: Do monopoles exist? Were they all inflated away?

items.reflection: Cabrera saw one event. Sagan said: 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.' When is one event ever enough?

moments.title: Franklin's lightning
moments.body: Franklin proposes lightning is electrical and proves it by flying a kite into a thunderstorm — extraordinarily risky; Georg Wilhelm Richmann died attempting a similar experiment in St Petersburg. Franklin introduces the terms 'positive' and 'negative' charge.
moments.takeaway: Lightning is electricity. The terminology Franklin invents is still used.

moments.title: Coulomb's law
moments.body: Coulomb uses a torsion balance to show electric force varies as 1/r^2 — exactly like Newton's gravity. The mathematical similarity hints at deep structure.
moments.takeaway: Electrostatics has the same inverse-square form as gravity.

moments.title: Galvani and Volta
moments.body: Galvani makes frog legs twitch with charged metals; he thinks the muscles store 'animal electricity'. Volta disagrees, showing it is the metals themselves; he builds the first battery (voltaic pile) in 1800.
moments.takeaway: The first source of steady electric current is invented.

moments.title: Millikan's oil drop
moments.body: Millikan measures the charge of the electron by watching charged oil droplets settle in an electric field. e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. Charge is quantised.
moments.takeaway: The electron's charge is measured directly. Millikan's notebooks were later found to omit some 'bad' data — a permanent ethical controversy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Coulomb's law and Millikan's measurement underpin all electrostatics. The electron charge is now defined exactly by the 2019 SI redefinition.
now.open_questions: Is the electron truly fundamental, or composite? Are charges precisely quantised by monopoles, or by another mechanism?

items.reflection: Millikan won a Nobel for the oil-drop experiment, but he selectively excluded data. Was it ethical? How do we evaluate historical scientists by modern standards?

moments.title: Einstein and stimulated emission
moments.body: Einstein derives the rates of absorption, spontaneous emission and a new process — stimulated emission. The latter sits dormant in textbooks for decades.
moments.takeaway: The basic principle of the laser is buried in a 1917 paper.

moments.title: Maser
moments.who: Charles Townes, James Gordon, Herbert Zeiger, Columbia
moments.body: Townes invents the ammonia maser — microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. He gets the idea on a park bench in Washington DC.
moments.takeaway: Coherent microwave amplification. The laser is one step away.

moments.title: Maiman's ruby laser
moments.body: Working with a ruby crystal and a flash tube from a photo shop, Maiman builds the first laser. His paper is rejected by Physical Review Letters; he publishes in Nature.
moments.takeaway: The first laser fits on a benchtop and is built with off-the-shelf parts.

moments.title: Lasers everywhere
moments.body: Lasers are in barcode scanners, fibre optics, eye surgery, DVD players, manufacturing, lithography (the entire semiconductor industry), laser cooling, gravitational-wave detectors, fusion ignition.
moments.takeaway: From novelty to ubiquity in 60 years.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Petawatt lasers reach intensities of 10^23 W/cm^2. Optical atomic clocks based on laser-cooled atoms reach 10^-19 precision. NIF lasers achieved fusion ignition in 2022.
now.open_questions: Can ultra-intense lasers probe nonlinear QED? Can laser-driven fusion be made commercial?

items.reflection: Maiman's paper was rejected by Physical Review Letters. How often do journals miss revolutionary work?

moments.title: Stefan's experimental law
moments.body: Stefan, examining experimental data, finds that total radiated power from a hot body scales as T^4. He uses the law to make the first reasonable estimate of the Sun's surface temperature (~5,700 K).
moments.takeaway: A T^4 law from experimental data alone.

moments.title: Boltzmann's thermodynamic derivation
moments.body: Boltzmann derives Stefan's law from classical thermodynamics — treating radiation as a gas with pressure P = u/3. The Stefan-Boltzmann law sigma T^4 is born.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical derivation backs up Stefan's empirical law.

moments.title: Wien's displacement law
moments.body: Wien shows the peak wavelength of blackbody radiation scales as 1/T. Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths. He wins the 1911 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Hotter is bluer. Wien's law lets us measure stellar temperatures from colour.

moments.title: Planck completes the picture
moments.body: Planck's quantum derivation of the blackbody curve subsumes both Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien as limiting cases. Classical thermodynamics is succeeded by quantum statistical mechanics.
moments.takeaway: Stefan, Boltzmann and Wien all follow from Planck's quantum hypothesis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Stefan-Boltzmann is central to climate models, stellar astrophysics, and thermal imaging. Earth's effective temperature (255 K) is too cold for liquid water without the greenhouse effect.
now.open_questions: How do clouds and aerosols modify Earth's effective radiating temperature?

items.reflection: Stefan derived a law from data alone. Planck derived it from a deep principle. Which kind of derivation is more 'scientific'?

moments.title: Boyle and Smith invent the CCD
moments.who: Willard Boyle, George Smith, Bell Labs
moments.body: At Bell Labs, Boyle and Smith sketch the charge-coupled device on a blackboard in an hour. The CCD shifts charge packets across a silicon chip — a quantum bucket brigade. They share the 2009 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Modern digital imaging is invented in an hour.

moments.title: First CCD camera in astronomy
moments.body: A CCD replaces photographic plates on a telescope. Quantum efficiency rises from ~1% (photography) to ~70%. Astronomy is transformed.
moments.takeaway: Astronomy becomes 70x more sensitive overnight.

moments.title: Hubble launched
moments.body: The Hubble Space Telescope launches with CCD cameras. Its images redefine public engagement with astronomy. The CCDs are roughly the resolution of an early phone camera.
moments.takeaway: A 1.5-MP camera takes the most iconic images in astronomy.

moments.title: Smartphone era
moments.body: CMOS sensors (a CCD descendant) make smartphone cameras ubiquitous. Roughly 4 billion smartphone cameras worldwide; users take ~1.7 trillion photos a year.
moments.takeaway: Quantum-mechanical photon counting becomes a consumer product.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: CMOS image sensors dominate. Modern cameras have 100+ megapixels. Direct-detection X-ray, EUV and infrared detectors all use silicon-based imaging.
now.open_questions: Can single-photon avalanche detector arrays beat CMOS in low light?

items.reflection: Boyle and Smith invented the CCD in an hour. How much modern technology rests on a few hours of inspiration?

moments.title: Lippershey's spyglass
moments.body: A Dutch spectacle-maker applies for a patent on a tube that makes distant things look near. The application is rejected as too simple to patent. Telescope-makers spring up across Europe.
moments.takeaway: The telescope is invented as a maritime toy.

moments.title: Galileo turns it skyward
moments.body:
Galileo improves the design to 30x magnification and points it at the heavens. In months he sees mountains on the Moon, four moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus, sunspots. He publishes 'Sidereus Nuncius'.

The geocentric universe is empirically wrong.
moments.takeaway: In one winter, Galileo transforms astronomy and threatens the Church's cosmology.

moments.title: Inquisition trials
moments.body: In 1616 the Church bans Copernicanism. Galileo, after publishing 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' in 1632, is tried by the Inquisition, forced to recant, and placed under house arrest for the rest of his life. He continues to work.
moments.takeaway: The Church silences but cannot reverse the scientific revolution.

moments.title: The Vatican apologises
moments.body: The Vatican formally acknowledges Galileo was right. The Church took 359 years to apologise.
moments.takeaway: Institutional admission of error takes centuries.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The JWST and ELT (39-m European telescope, first light 2028) extend Galileo's work to billions of light years. Adaptive optics correct atmospheric blur. Space-based telescopes resolve features billions of times finer than Galileo's first sketches.
now.open_questions: Can ELT/HabEx directly image Earth-like exoplanets?

items.reflection: Galileo recanted to save his life but reportedly muttered 'Eppur si muove' — 'and yet it moves'. When should a scientist compromise to survive?

moments.title: Gilbert's 'De Magnete'
moments.body: Physician to Queen Elizabeth I, Gilbert publishes the first scientific treatise on magnetism. He shows the Earth itself is a giant magnet, explaining why compasses point north. He coins the term 'electricity' (electricus, from amber).
moments.takeaway: The first quantitative book on electromagnetism, and the first identification of Earth as a magnet.

moments.title: Magnetic survey expeditions
moments.body: Halley charts magnetic declination across the Atlantic. Gauss in 1839 derives the spherical-harmonic decomposition of Earth's field. Magnetic observatories spring up worldwide.
moments.takeaway: Geomagnetism becomes a mature science before its mechanism is understood.

moments.title: Reversals discovered
moments.body: Brunhes finds volcanic rocks magnetised in the wrong direction. The Earth's magnetic field has flipped — and many times. Reversals are confirmed by 1960s seafloor surveys.
moments.takeaway: Earth's poles have flipped hundreds of times. We're 780,000 years overdue for the next.

moments.title: Van Allen belts
moments.body: Explorer 1, the first US satellite, carries Van Allen's Geiger counter. The instrument saturates — Earth has belts of trapped radiation. The discovery essentially launches space physics.
moments.takeaway: Space exploration immediately reveals a new feature of Earth's magnetic environment.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Earth's field is generated by a self-sustaining geodynamo in the liquid outer core. The field has been weakening 5% per century. ESA's Swarm satellite mission monitors it.
now.open_questions: When will Earth's next magnetic reversal occur? Could it harm life or technology?

items.reflection: Gilbert in 1600 thought magnetism was the 'soul' of the Earth. He was wrong in detail, right in spirit. How should we evaluate metaphors in early science?

moments.title: Fourier's heat equation
moments.body: Fourier's 'Théorie analytique de la chaleur' includes the diffusion equation for heat flow — q = -k dT/dx. The equation generalises to all diffusion processes.
moments.takeaway: Heat conduction obeys a partial differential equation.

moments.title: Kelvin's age of Earth
moments.body: Kelvin uses Fourier's heat equation to calculate how long Earth has been cooling from a molten state. His answer: 20-400 million years. This contradicts Darwin's biology and Lyell's geology, which demand hundreds of millions or billions of years.
moments.takeaway: Heat conduction is used to attack evolutionary biology.

moments.title: Curies measure radium's heat
moments.body: Radium continuously generates heat — a previously unknown energy source. Rutherford realises radioactive heating inside Earth invalidates Kelvin's calculation; Earth can be much older.
moments.takeaway: Kelvin's argument collapses; Earth is 4.5 billion years old.

moments.title: Earth's age measured
moments.body: Patterson dates meteorites with uranium-lead chronology and gets 4.55 ± 0.07 billion years. The biologists were right; Kelvin was wrong.
moments.takeaway: Radioactivity solves the age-of-Earth controversy in the geologists' favour.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Earth is 4.54 billion years old. Heat conduction equations describe thermal management in CPUs, building insulation, planetary interiors and stellar atmospheres.
now.open_questions: How much of Earth's interior heat is primordial vs radiogenic?

items.reflection: Kelvin was a giant who used impeccable thermodynamics — and was wrong. What does that say about confidence in our own current best models?

moments.title: Tsiolkovsky's equation
moments.body: A deaf Russian schoolteacher publishes the rocket equation: Δv = v_e ln(m_0/m_f). He shows that escaping Earth requires multi-stage rockets and liquid propellants. He dies in 1935 without seeing a single rocket fly.
moments.takeaway: Spaceflight is mathematically possible. Tsiolkovsky shows it 50 years before Sputnik.

moments.title: Goddard's first liquid rocket
moments.body: Goddard's first liquid-fuel rocket flies 12.5 m. The New York Times mocks him. In 1969 the Times publishes a retraction the day after Apollo 11 launches.
moments.takeaway: Goddard is ridiculed for proposing rockets in space. The Times apologises 43 years later.

moments.title: V-2 reaches space
moments.body: Nazi Germany's V-2 ballistic missile crosses the Kármán line — the first human-made object in space. Built with slave labour, it kills more workers in its construction than in its targets.
moments.takeaway: Spaceflight is born as a weapon.

moments.title: Sputnik to the Moon
moments.body: Sputnik (1957), Gagarin (1961), Apollo 11 (1969) — humans reach orbit, then the Moon, in 12 years. All using Tsiolkovsky's equation.
moments.takeaway: From paper equation to lunar landing in 66 years.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Reusable rockets (SpaceX) lower the cost per kg to orbit by ~10x. ~10,000 satellites are in orbit (2025). Starship aims at Mars; the Artemis programme returns humans to the Moon.
now.open_questions: Can chemical rockets reach interstellar space? Can fusion or antimatter propulsion become real?

items.reflection: Tsiolkovsky was deaf, isolated and self-taught. Goddard was ridiculed by the New York Times. Why does establishment opinion so often dismiss what becomes mainstream?

moments.title: Pauli's desperate proposal
moments.body: Beta decay seems to violate energy conservation. Pauli proposes a neutral, near-massless particle — the 'neutron' (he later calls it neutrino, 'little neutral one'). He famously writes: 'I have done a terrible thing, I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected.'
moments.takeaway: Pauli postulates a particle he believes nobody will ever see.

moments.title: Cowan and Reines detect neutrinos
moments.body: At the Savannah River nuclear reactor, Cowan and Reines detect the inverse beta decay of antineutrinos. They send Pauli a telegram. He responds: 'Thanks for message. Everything comes to him who knows how to wait.'
moments.takeaway: Pauli's 'undetectable' particle is detected 26 years later.

moments.title: Three neutrino flavours
moments.body: Brookhaven experiments show the muon has its own neutrino, different from the electron's. By 2000, the tau neutrino is also confirmed.
moments.takeaway: Three neutrino flavours match three lepton families.

moments.title: Neutrino oscillation
moments.body: Super-K shows atmospheric muon neutrinos transforming into tau neutrinos as they traverse Earth. SNO confirms solar electron neutrinos transform too. Neutrinos have mass — contradicting the original Standard Model.
moments.takeaway: Neutrinos oscillate. They have mass. The Standard Model is incomplete.

moments.title: Nobel for oscillation
moments.body: The 2015 Nobel goes to the Super-K and SNO leaders for proving neutrinos oscillate.
moments.takeaway: Neutrino mass is the first proven physics beyond the Standard Model.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Neutrino mass is < 0.8 eV (KATRIN, 2022). The mass hierarchy and CP violation in neutrinos are major experimental goals (DUNE, Hyper-K). About 100 trillion solar neutrinos pass through your body every second.
now.open_questions: Are neutrinos their own antiparticles (Majorana)? Why are their masses so small?

items.reflection: Pauli postulated an undetectable particle to save energy conservation. Was this sound science or special pleading?

moments.title: Ohm's law
moments.body: Ohm publishes V = IR. The work is initially dismissed by the German physics establishment; Ohm loses his teaching post. He is vindicated in 1841 with the Copley Medal of the Royal Society.
moments.takeaway: A schoolteacher's empirical law is rejected, then becomes a foundational principle.

moments.title: Drude's electron gas
moments.body: Drude models metals as a gas of free electrons bouncing off positive ions. He derives Ohm's law and the Wiedemann-Franz law linking thermal and electrical conductivity.
moments.takeaway: Classical electron gas explains metallic conduction — approximately.

moments.title: Sommerfeld's quantum metal
moments.body: Sommerfeld replaces Drude's Maxwell-Boltzmann electrons with Fermi-Dirac quantum statistics. Most low-T failures of Drude are resolved.
moments.takeaway: Quantum statistics fix the classical metal theory.

moments.title: Quantum Hall effect
moments.body: Von Klitzing finds Hall resistance is quantised in exact units of h/e^2 — a topological effect. He wins the 1985 Nobel. The constant is now used to define the kilogram (SI 2019).
moments.takeaway: Resistance is quantised exactly, by topology. The kilogram becomes a resistance.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Topological insulators, Weyl semimetals and exotic conductors are studied worldwide. Quantum Hall metrology defines SI electrical units. Superconducting wires move TWh-scale power without loss in pilot projects.
now.open_questions: Can topological qubits be built? Can room-temperature SC be engineered?

items.reflection: Ohm lost his job for publishing his law. How often do new ideas get punished before being accepted?

moments.title: Coriolis derives the force
moments.body: Coriolis, studying water wheels, derives the deflection of motion in a rotating reference frame: -2 m omega x v. He had no idea his result would dominate atmospheric science.
moments.takeaway: A mechanical engineer's water-wheel insight ends up explaining weather.

moments.title: Foucault's pendulum
moments.body: Foucault hangs a 67-m pendulum in the Panthéon. The plane of swing slowly rotates — about 11° per hour at Paris's latitude. This is a direct demonstration that the Earth rotates beneath the pendulum.
moments.takeaway: Earth's rotation is visible in a single afternoon.

moments.title: Buys Ballot's law
moments.body: Stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere: low pressure is on your left. The empirical rule formalises how Coriolis force creates the global pattern of weather.
moments.takeaway: Weather patterns are organised by Earth's rotation.

moments.title: Numerical weather prediction
moments.body: Modern weather forecasts solve the rotating-frame Navier-Stokes equations on planetary grids with 1-10 km resolution. Coriolis terms are essential at every step.
moments.takeaway: Coriolis is built into every weather forecast on Earth.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: GFS, ECMWF and Met Office models forecast weather days to weeks ahead. ML weather models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather) match physical models at lower cost. All require Coriolis.
now.open_questions: Can subseasonal prediction be made reliable? How important is detailed cloud resolution?

items.reflection: The Coriolis 'force' isn't a real force — it's a consequence of choosing a rotating frame. When is a fictitious force a useful description vs a confusion?

moments.title: Zwicky's missing mass
moments.body: Zwicky measures velocities of galaxies in the Coma cluster. They move so fast they should fly apart unless there is ~400x more mass than the visible stars provide. He calls it 'dunkle Materie' — dark matter. He is ignored for 40 years.
moments.takeaway: Dark matter is hypothesised in 1933. The community files it under 'eccentric Zwicky'.

moments.title: Vera Rubin's rotation curves
moments.who: Vera Rubin, Kent Ford, DTM Washington
moments.body: Rubin measures the rotation of dozens of spiral galaxies. The outer stars move just as fast as the inner ones — they should be slower if Newtonian gravity from visible mass were all. Most galactic mass must be dark.
moments.takeaway: Dark matter is decisively established. Rubin is never awarded the Nobel.

moments.title: First strong gravitational lens
moments.body: Twin quasars Q0957+561 turn out to be one quasar imaged twice by an intervening galaxy. The galaxy's mass — much more than its stars — bends light.
moments.takeaway: Gravitational lensing weighs galaxies — and confirms dark matter.

moments.title: Bullet Cluster
moments.body: X-ray and lensing observations of the Bullet Cluster show the visible gas and the mass have separated after a collision. Dark matter passes through; gas does not. The result is among the strongest evidence for dark matter as a particle.
moments.takeaway: Dark matter behaves like a collisionless particle, not modified gravity.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Dark matter makes up 27% of the universe and 84% of all matter. Direct detection (XENONnT, LZ, PandaX) has so far found nothing. Indirect searches (Fermi, IceCube) likewise.
now.open_questions: What is dark matter? WIMPs, axions, primordial black holes?

items.reflection: Rubin's contribution is monumental and uncontested. She was never awarded the Nobel. The asteroid 5726 Rubin is named for her. Is naming planets and prizes for women a substitute for, or supplement to, real equity?
